activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: In a model with two goods, one country cannot have a comparative advantage in both, because a lower opportunity cost for one good means a higher opportunity cost for the other.
story:
Connor had set the lemonade stand on the gravel drive at his grandfather's, two card tables pushed together, a hand-lettered sign, and a cooler of ice sweating in the July heat. On the second table his little sister Ruth had spread her own inventory: four sad-looking sugar cookies and a jar of lemonade she'd made from a mix. The plan had been to split the profits, though so far the profits were two dollars and a mosquito bite.

"You're ruining our brand," Connor said, pointing at the mix jar, which was the color of highlighter.

"You're ruining our brand," Ruth said back, without looking up from her rock collection, and that was the whole morning until Grandfather came out with the newspaper and a folding chair and planted himself where he could supervise and mock in equal measure.

The argument started over Japan, or rather over a YouTube video Ruth had watched at two in the morning. "They could be better at everything," she declared, sprinkling gravel onto a cookie like powdered sugar. "Cars, cookies, lemonade, all of it. Some country is just the best at everything in every sense."

"Every sense," Connor repeated, because it was a ridiculous thing to say and he wanted to hear her defend it.

"Every single sense."

Grandfather lowered the newspaper an inch. He had a way of treating grandchildren's disputes as spectator sports. "Here's a question, Ruthie," he said. "If Japan makes a car and a cookie, what does it give up to make the cookie?"

Ruth frowned. "Nothing. Cookies are easy."

"Compared to what?"

"Compared to us making cookies."

"And when you make a cookie instead of a car, what do you give up?"

"I can't make a car," Ruth said, with dignity. "I'm eleven."

"You give up almost nothing, then," Grandfather said, and folded the paper shut, satisfied, as if this settled things, which it did not settle things in Connor's head at all. It sat inchoate there for a while, a shape he couldn't name, while Ruth sold her highlighter lemonade to the mail carrier for fifty cents and Connor's fresh-squeezed pitcher went untouched, which stung, because his cost more to make and it was objectively better.

He did the math on the back of the sign while Ruth counted her quarters. His lemonade cost him maybe a dollar a cup in lemons and time. Hers cost a quarter. If a customer bought from her instead of him, the customer gave up very little by not buying his, but if he spent an hour squeezing lemons, he gave up the hour he could have spent baking cookies, which nobody at this stand was doing, which meant the cookies were scarce, which meant Ruth could charge what she liked for those gravel-dusted little pucks. He thought about Grandfather's question, turned it over, and felt something click into place like a lawn chair snapping open. If it cost him less to make lemonade than cookies, it had to cost him more to make cookies than lemonade. It worked both directions at once, like a seesaw. You couldn't be the one who gives up less for both things, because giving up less for one meant giving up more for the other. He tried to break it, sliding numbers around, looking for a country better at everything in every sense, and the seesaw kept tipping. One of them had to be the cheap cookie, one of them the cheap car.

"There's a word for this," he announced. "Comparative advantage."

"Bless you," said Grandfather.

"Nobody can have it in both things. That's the whole point. Even if Japan's better at everything in every sense, like Ruth says, it still gives up more to make the cheap thing, so we should make the cheap thing and trade." He was talking fast now, waving a wooden spoon. "Ruth, you make cookies. I make lemonade. We trade at a price in between."

Ruth considered this with the gravity of a merchant queen. "One cookie per lemonade, and I keep the mail carrier money."

"Extortion," said Connor, but he shook on it, and Grandfather laughed so hard he had to adjust his chair.

The afternoon taught Connor two further lessons. One was that trading a superior product for a cookie with gravel on it felt, in a small way, like complicity, and he understood for the first time that every deal probably felt like that from one side. The other was that their mother had spent years trying to inculcate basic hygiene in Ruth, and it had not taken, because Ruth licked each cookie once before selling it, claiming this "sealed the flavor." The mail carrier, returning for a second lemonade, watched the sealing process with visible alarm and bought the lemonade anyway.

They counted the till at sunset: six dollars and change, mostly quarters. Grandfather said the whole enterprise had taught them more than a semester of school, which Connor doubted, since schools had desks and nobody licked the desks. But driving home with the empty cooler rattling in the trunk, he kept turning the seesaw over in his mind, testing it against real countries he knew nothing about, wondering where the model stopped working, whether it held with more than two goods, whether anyone had ever checked. He didn't know. He liked not knowing, a little.

"So next weekend," Ruth said from the back seat, "I do the lemonade, you do the cookies."

"I don't know how to bake."

"Then you'll give up a lot of cookies," she said. "Sounds like a you problem."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A half cadence ends a phrase on the V chord, which sounds unfinished and makes the listener expect another phrase to follow.
story:
Elliot arrived at Ms. Okafor's studio on Tuesday with sixteen blank bars of staff paper and a deadline: the composition was due Friday, performed at the youth recital, no exceptions. He had three weeks of theory behind him and one finished bar, a little rising figure in C major that he liked so much he had played it forty times and now suspected everyone else was sick of it.

"You've written one bar," Ms. Okafor said, looking at the page. She was not scolding. She never scolded; she just described things with terrible accuracy, which was worse.

"It's a good bar," Elliot said. "It does a lot."

"It does one thing. It goes up." She spun the bench toward the piano. "Play it with a chord under it. C major. Then try G. Tell me which one makes you want to keep going."

He played the melody over the C chord and it sounded finished, boxed in, like a bug under glass. Over G it leaned forward, tugging at something that wasn't there yet. He played both twice more, mostly because he liked the second one and partly to delay admitting she'd made a point.

"There," she said. "That lean. That's what chords do to a melody. Your job this week is to choose the lean, bar by bar. You have to notate it properly, chord symbols above the staff, no mysteries. And eighth bar especially. The eighth bar is where a phrase ends, so the eighth bar is where you either let the listener breathe or you don't."

That night Elliot sat at the kitchen table with the manuscript paper and a plate of crackers that did nothing to assuage the feeling that he had no idea what he was doing. His little sister June, eight years old and incurably nosy, read over his shoulder while eating his crackers one by one.

"Why does your music have letters above it," she said. "Is it spelling something."

"It's telling the piano player what chords to use. It's like a recipe."

"Spell a word in it."

"June. It's due Friday."

She spelled PIZZA into the chord line, which meant bars six and seven were now labeled with nonsense, and he had to redo them, and in redoing them he accidentally discovered that if he put G under bar eight, the whole first half of the melody felt like a question. It hung there. It wanted a second half. He didn't know why it worked, only that it did, the way a door left open a crack makes you walk over and look through it.

On Thursday his friend Deshawn, who took lessons at the same studio and was quietly, obnoxiously better than everyone, texted him: "done with mine. 16 bars. ended on the I chord, big and final, teacher will love it. how's yours going." Elliot typed "great" and then deleted it, because it was a lie, and then typed "half done" and stared at it. That was technically true in a way Deshawn would never guess.

At Friday's lesson Ms. Okafor played his sixteen bars straight through, twice. The first time she kept going past bar eight as if she hadn't noticed it, and the second time she stopped exactly on the G chord and let it hang in the room. Elliot held his breath. She was famously taciturn; students had a running joke that she once went an entire lesson saying only "again," and he braced for another "again."

Instead she said, "You ended the eighth bar on the V chord. Do you know what that's called?"

"Um. A hanging-up thing?"

"A half cadence," she said. "It ends the phrase on the V chord, which sounds unfinished, and makes the listener expect another phrase to follow. Which is why I just spent the last thirty seconds expecting one."

"So that's bad?"

"So that's a choice. You made half your piece feel like a sentence with no period." She tapped bar eight. "And then you gave them the second phrase, and you ended the whole thing on C. So the question you delayed got answered. Some composers would say that's the whole game." She looked at him with what he chose to interpret as approval. "Where did you learn that?"

"June spelled pizza on my chord line."

"I won't ask."

At the recital that evening, seven students played their compositions. Deshawn's ended enormous and final, the I chord like a door slamming, and the audience clapped big and immediate. Elliot's ended after its hanging question, after the lean, and the applause came half a beat late, as if people had been waiting for one more phrase that never arrived. Deshawn found him afterward by the punch bowl.

"Yours did the lean thing at the middle," Deshawn said. "I was waiting for more and then it just ended. It was kind of annoying."

"That was kind of the plan," Elliot said, and felt a small, ridiculous pride in having annoyed a room full of strangers on purpose.

Ms. Okafor passed by with a stack of programs. "Elliot," she said, without stopping, "next time, thirty-two bars."

He looked at his empty punch cup, then at June, who was sitting in the front row trying to spell something on the recital program with her finger. "I think," he told Deshawn, "I'm going to need more crackers."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: In Java, a field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class.
story:
Oliver got to the lab early enough to claim the machine by the window, the one whose fan didn't rattle like a dying animal, and he had just opened his project when Priya slid into the seat beside him with her laptop already on. Coding club met Tuesdays in the back corner of the library annex, six or seven students and a whiteboard that still bore someone's abandoned diagram of a recursive function, a snake eating its own tail. Tonight's task, written on the whiteboard in Ms. Reyes's tidy capitals, was to build a BankAccount class in Java, with a balance and an owner name, and then write tests for it. Oliver had a reason for caring about this particular assignment that he hadn't told anyone: he'd applied for a summer internship that required basic Java, and the rejection email had arrived on Saturday, polite and impervious, wishing him well in his future endeavors.

He started with the fields. He typed them the way the textbook showed, the word private in front of each one, then wrote the constructor, then paused. Priya was typing faster, the way she always did, her screen filling with code the way an aquifer fills a well dug in the right place, steadily and without apparent effort. Oliver slowed down on purpose. His father, who repaired boilers for a living, had a rule he'd repeated the summer Oliver was twelve, kneeling beside him on a kitchen floor with a wrench and a leaking pipe: you don't get to skip the boring part, because the boring part is where you find out what's actually broken. Oliver had hated that sentence at twelve. He had thought about it all through the internship application, which he'd rushed, and which had gone out with a portfolio he now suspected was half-finished in exactly the places he'd been bored.

"Done," Priya announced, fifteen minutes in, and spun her laptop toward the test file. "Watch, this will pass on the first run." It didn't. The compiler refused her code outright, underlining a line in red and refusing to produce anything runnable. She stared at it, then clicked build again, as though the error were an impugnment of her character that the machine would withdraw on reflection.

Oliver leaned over. Her test tried to read the balance field directly, something like account.balance, straight out of the object, no method call. The error message used words like "has private access." He read it twice, and something clicked into place, the way a diagram clicks when you stop skimming. The fields were locked. The word at the front of each declaration, the one he'd copied out of habit, wasn't decoration.

"It's private," he said. "The fields. They're private."

"So what, I wrote them, they're mine."

"Look at the message." He pointed at the red line. "A field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class. Your test is a different class. It's outside."

Priya frowned at the screen, and Oliver watched her go through the same small collapse and rebuild he'd gone through thirty seconds earlier, the flush and then the recalibration. She wasn't stupid; she was faster than he was, and being fast had never once required her to stop and look at what a word actually did. He almost didn't say the next part, because the next part was the twist he hadn't expected of himself: he knew how to fix it, and he wanted to be the one to fix it, and he also wanted not to want that.

"You can add a getter," he said, more quietly than he'd intended. "A method inside the class that returns the balance. Then the test calls the method instead of reaching into the field directly."

She was already typing. getBalance, public, one line. The test compiled, ran, passed, and she sat back with the particular exhale of someone whose code has finally obeyed. "That's so roundabout, though. Why lock a thing and then hand out the key on a string?"

Oliver turned back to his own screen and tried the experiment from the other side. He wrote his fields private, wrote getters, and then, deliberately, wrote one test that tried to grab the balance directly, and one that changed it through a deposit method with a guard against negative amounts. The direct grab died at compile time; the deposit went through, and the guard caught the negative value exactly as designed. The second error, the runtime one, was the kind that mattered, the kind that told you something real about the world instead of just about your syntax. He sat with that for a moment. The lock wasn't about keeping secrets from yourself. It was about making sure that every change passed through the door where you'd put the guard.

"I don't totally get it either," he admitted. "Like, if you're the one writing both classes, who are you protecting it from?"

"Future you," Priya said. "Future you is an idiot. Present me can tell you that from experience."

Ms. Reyes drifted past their table, looked at the green PASS lines on two screens, and wrote something on her clipboard without comment. Oliver opened the internship email again, read it one more time, and then closed it and started drafting the message he'd been avoiding for four days, asking whether applicants could reapply for the spring session. He had the getter method open beside the blank message, one line, returning something worth keeping.

"Hey," Priya said. "Tuesday. You're explaining interfaces. You clearly read ahead."

"I read ahead slowly," Oliver said, and hit send.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Stage left and stage right are named from the actor's point of view while facing the audience, so they are the reverse of the audience's left and right.
story:
Marcus pushed the coffee table against the wall and rolled the rug into the corner, and by noon his living room had become a stage, or the idea of one, marked out in masking tape from his mother's junk drawer. The one-act was his: chosen from a stack of scripts the drama club left behind in June, cast with two friends from his graduating class, and scheduled to perform in the school's black box theater the last weekend of August, before everyone scattered to colleges in four different states. He had acted in plays for four years, so he knew what directors did in the way you know what surgeons do from watching hospital shows. Now he had to actually do it.

Dara arrived first, carrying a water bottle and an apology for Priya, who was fifteen minutes behind because her brother had the car. Dara played the sister in the play, the one who stays. Marcus had a spiral notebook with a hand-drawn floor plan and numbered scenes, and on the floor plan he had written L and R in the margins with confident little arrows. He had spent two evenings on that plan, imagining how the audience at the school would see the two women cross toward each other in the final scene, and the arrows were the product of that imagining.

They worked the opening scene, and it went badly in the ordinary way, lines dropped, laughs at the wrong moments, until Priya arrived and they ran it again and something caught. When Dara turned her back on Priya at the fourth line and held still for a breath too long, Marcus felt the room change temperature. "Keep that," he said, standing up from the couch he'd pushed to the window. "That pause. That's the whole play, kind of." Dara nodded, but she looked at the script like she wanted to write it down, and he made himself say it again plainly so she could.

Then he called his first real blocking note. "Okay, in the argument, when you say 'You never once asked,' I want you to walk away from her. Go left." Dara went left, from where Marcus stood by the couch, and the shape of the scene collapsed: she ended up downstage of Priya, her back to the imagined audience, the confrontation smothered. He said left again, pointing, and she crossed further the wrong way, and Priya laughed once, not unkindly. They argued about whose left, and Marcus's pugnacious first instinct, that they were both being deliberately dense, lasted about ten seconds before a cold thought arrived: maybe the fault was his.

He went to the tape line at the edge of the rug and stood on it, facing the empty room the way an actor would face an audience, and looked down at his own hands. "Say left again," he told Priya, and when she did, he watched which way his own body wanted to move. It was the opposite of the direction he'd been pointing from the couch. He stepped off the line, feeling the idea settle, not explained but demonstrated, true the way a door is true when it opens. "Stage left and stage right are from the actor's point of view, facing the audience," he said. "So they're the reverse of the audience's left and right." Dara mouthed backwards to herself, walked back to her mark, and when he called the note again she moved clean across the space, and suddenly the final image worked from both sides, the one who leaves exiting away from the one who stays.

He wrote it in the notebook in block letters, a small private ceremony, then made them run the scene four more times. He had always thought of directing as control, as knowing the answer in advance, and some of it was that, the floor plan and the numbered scenes, the way you burnish a line by repeating it until it shines. But the afternoon had also been something else, more like homeostasis, the way a body returns itself to temperature after a shock: Dara's held breath, the wrong-way crossing, the correction, the room finding its level again through all three of them at once. He didn't have a word for the second thing and suspected that naming it would make it smaller.

They broke at six for pizza on the porch, and Priya asked whether he was nervous, twenty minutes into the conversation, apropos of nothing, which meant she was nervous herself. He said yes. He told them he'd been certain this morning and was less certain now, and that this felt like progress, though he couldn't prove it. Dara said the last scene still didn't land, the very end, where the script only says she sits. He said he'd think about it. He got up, went back inside, and stood alone at the tape line facing the empty room, and tried, for a long moment, to watch the scene as the audience would.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Hormonal IUDs and contraceptive implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once placed by a clinician they do not depend on daily use.
story:
The waiting room had five chairs and a poster about chlamydia that Grace had read four times before the door with the frosted window opened. "Grace? You're the new peer educator from Roosevelt, right? I'm Dana." The nurse held the door, and Grace stood, smoothing her backpack strap as if it were the thing being evaluated.

The exam room was small, a paper-covered table nobody was using, a plastic model of a uterus on the counter that Dana nudged aside to make room for a shoebox of brochures. "So the health center wants students who can talk to other students about the basics. Consent, contraception, where to get tested. You'll do tables at lunch once you're trained." Grace nodded, though the nod felt premature. She had signed up because Priya had signed up, and then Priya's family had moved in March, and now the whole thing sat in Grace's hands alone.

"Start wherever you want," Dana said. "Pretend I'm a student who walked up to your table."

"Okay. Um. Consent means yes, and only yes counts, and it has to be sober and you can take it back." The words came out in a rehearsed clump, the way she'd practiced on the bus, and Dana tilted her head. "Good bones. Now say it to me like I asked because my boyfriend says I owe him since we've been dating a year."

Grace blinked. That was not the question she had rehearsed. "I'd say... you don't owe it because of time. That's like saying a ride to school obligates you to anything later."

"Nice. Some people call that reasoning sophistry, arguments that sound logical but exist to wear you down. His logic is a tool, not a truth." Dana said it lightly, but Grace wrote it in her notebook, underlined twice, because she had heard versions of that argument in the hallway said confidently enough to pass for sense.

"For contraception," Grace said, moving on, "there's the pill, and condoms, and I think the shot?"

"What would you tell a student who asks which is best?"

"The pill. It's the most... it's what everyone says is most effective. Ninety-nine percent." She felt steady saying it, since she had looked it up just last night, which was why the pause that followed felt like a trapdoor.

Dana pulled two things from the drawer: a small T-shaped device and a matchstick-sized rod. "This is a hormonal IUD, this is an implant. Can you guess how they compare to the pill in real use?"

"Real use?"

"Think about the pill. What does it depend on?"

Grace looked at the plastic T, turning it over. "Taking it every day. Which people... don't. School, travel, forgetting." She was thinking of her cousin's story, the spring nobody in the family talked about directly, the one that had made her mother go quiet when Grace mentioned the peer ed program. "So the pill's number is how it works if you're perfect, and real people aren't perfect."

"There it is," Dana said, but didn't elaborate, which Grace found both irritating and respectful. She picked up the implant instead, rolling it between her fingers.

"So this doesn't depend on remembering anything. Once it's in, it's in." She was working it aloud, watching Dana's face for signals. "So is the real-world number closer to the perfect one?"

"Hormonal IUDs and implants fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year," Dana said, taking the brochure from the box and sliding it across. "Because once placed by a clinician, they don't depend on daily use. The pill's typical number is way off its perfect number. These two barely move."

Grace read the brochure twice. Fewer than one in a hundred. A year. Placed by a clinician. She had repeated the ninety-nine percent figure at dinner on Tuesday as though she'd known something, and the certainty she'd felt then seemed, in this small room, like a borrowed coat. "So when Priya and I made that poster, the one that ranked the pill first, we were..."

"Ranking by the number on the box instead of the number in a life," Dana said. "Happens constantly."

Grace thought about that for a moment, the gap between a statistic and a person holding it. Was effectiveness something extrinsic to the method, she wondered, something that lived partly in the morning routine, the backpack, the alarm clock? The question felt too large for a notebook, but she wrote it anyway.

"What about testing?" she asked. "For infections."

"Same as everything else. You tell them it's a urine test or a swab, results in a week, free here, no notification of parents for STI services in this state at your age. And you tell them getting tested isn't an accusation of anybody. It's maintenance. Like an oil change."

"Nobody calls an oil change a judgment on your driving."

"Exactly that."

They ran through scenarios for another half hour, Dana playing a girl who was scared, a boy who was blustery, a student who asked whether the clinic would tell coach. Grace fumbled the scared one, softened too fast, then over-corrected into stiffness. "You'll find the middle," Dana said. "It takes a semester."

On her way out, Grace stopped at the model uterus, still sitting on the counter, and picked up the little T-shaped device one more time, turning it under the fluorescent light, this plain object that did its work by staying put.

"You can take one for your table," Dana said. "Display only."

Grace dropped it into the side pocket of her backpack, where it clicked against her pens. "Can I come back Thursday? I want to redo the poster before anyone else sees it."

"Thursday's fine," Dana said, already opening the door for the next patient. "Bring the poster."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent.
story:
Cole's uncle Ray had converted the garage into a shrine to the driving test: a strip of masking tape across the concrete floor, two plastic cones borrowed from a road crew, and a folding chair where Ray sat eating sunflower seeds and offering commentary.

"Again," Ray said, spitting a shell into a coffee can. "You're six inches from the curb, but you parked like you were apologizing to the car behind you. Confidence, Cole. The cones can smell fear."

Cole backed up again, hands at ten and two, checking his mirrors more often than the situation required because checking mirrors was the one thing he knew he was good at. The test was in nine days. His mother had transcribed the whole driver's manual onto index cards and quizzed him at dinner, and he could recite right-of-way rules like scripture, but the cards had not made his hands any steadier.

"The highway's what worries me," he said over the whine of reverse. "Merging. Everybody speeding up, nobody letting you in."

"You've got a turn signal and a functioning face. People respond to both." Ray cracked another seed. "Tomorrow we do the real thing. Loop around town, get on 94, hit the construction by Miller Road."

The next afternoon they sat in slow traffic, orange barrels narrowing two lanes into one, and Cole's problem arrived in its true form. A line of cars had already moved into the right lane, stretching back a quarter mile, while the left lane stood empty and forbidden-looking. He signalled early and nosed in behind a pickup.

"Or," Ray said, "you could stay in this lane."

"That's cheating. Those people waited."

"Is it?"

Cole glanced at the pickup driver in his mirror, then at the open lane. "It feels like cutting in line. Like being that kid at lunch."

"You're the one always quoting statistics at me. What do you actually know about this?"

Cole chewed on it, literally, working a sunflower seed like his uncle. He remembered something he'd read while flipping through a state website instead of the manual, a fact he'd dismissed as trivia and now couldn't dismiss at all. "Minnesota's Department of Transportation," he said slowly, "says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as forty percent."

"So?"

"So it's not cutting. It's what they want you to do. It's official." He pulled back into the left lane, feeling like a criminal with a permit, and drove all the way to the cones, where a woman in a hatchback waved him in with an almost cheerful gesture of surrender.

"There," Ray said. "You just zipped."

"I still feel like a jerk."

"You can feel like a jerk and be right. Welcome to driving."

They merged onto the highway a mile later and Cole pressed the accelerator with more nerve than he'd managed in any garage drill, matching speed, sliding into a gap between a semi and a sedan whose driver did not honk, which felt like applause.

That night he looked it up again to check the fact's veracity, because the internet had told him things before that turned out to be folklore dressed as data, and found he'd had it right. He sat with that for a while. The rules of the road and the ethics of the lunch line were supposed to be the same thing, and it bothered him that they weren't, that what looked rude could be what everyone needed done. He decided, provisionally, the way he decided most things, that he'd zipper merge when the signs said to and feel only fifty percent like a jerk about it, and that the other fifty percent he'd work on.

The morning of the test, Ray handed him the keys in the garage, between the cones. "Parallel park it one more time. For luck."

Cole backed in on the first try, close and clean, and stopped with the bumper a graceful inch from the tape.

"Was that confidence," Ray asked, "or did you just memorize where the curb is?"

Cole grinned and pulled the seatbelt across his chest. "Both lanes," he said. "All the way to the merge point. Wish me luck."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: US inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980 and fell below 3 percent by 1983, after the Federal Reserve's sharp interest rate increases.
story:
The lemonade stand stood at the end of the Drapers' driveway because their corner got the traffic from the pool, and Clara had claimed it in June with a hand-lettered sign and a folding table that wobbled on one leg. By late July the stand had become something else too, a place where she and Theo spread out his binder and her notebook between the pitcher and the cash box, because Theo's mother worked until six and his house had no air conditioning and, as Theo put it, the lemonade stand at least had shade. Their economics quiz was tomorrow morning, first period, and the graph was still defeating them.

"Here," Clara said, turning the binder so it faced him across the table. The line climbed a mountain and then fell off a cliff. "Inflation, percent, 1970 to 1990. Explain the cliff. Mrs. Okafor says if we can't say why it drops there, we don't understand the whole unit." A woman in a sun hat paused at the curb, and Clara poured a cup without being asked, added ice, made change from the box, and turned back before the woman had reached the next driveway.

Theo was the smarter one in most subjects and knew it, which was why he hated this. "It just falls," he said. "Something happened. A law, maybe. Prices got capped."

"No." Clara said it more firmly than she meant to. "Look at the axis. It peaks at 14.8 percent in March 1980. Then by 1983 it's below 3 percent. That's not a law. We read about this. The Fed raised interest rates, sharply, and that's the drop." She had written it on an index card two nights ago and then lost confidence in the card, because she could recite the sentence and still not feel she owned it. Reciting was one thing. She had spent four years of debate tournaments perfecting an elocution that could make any sentence sound certain, and she was beginning to suspect that this talent was a trap.

"Fine," Theo said. "But she'll ask us to say why. Why does raising rates do it? You always say the why is the quiz."

Down the street a sprinkler ticked in an arc, and a small kid on a bicycle stopped to watch them argue, which reminded Clara that the stand was still technically a business. "One dollar," she told the kid, who dug in a pocket and produced quarters counted out one at a time, licked and sticky. She waited, patient, because the kid was impecunious in the way all eleven-year-olds in August are, holding his whole fortune in coins, and a dollar for cold lemonade was still a fair trade. He drank it standing up and rode off.

"Okay," she said, sitting back down. "Try it this way. I'm the Fed. You're everybody borrowing money." She held up the pitcher. "The price of this, of borrowing, goes up. So what do you do?"

Theo frowned. "Buy less of it. Fewer loans. Fewer people buying houses, businesses expanding."

"And if fewer people are buying, what do sellers do?"

There was a pause, the kind where she could watch someone assemble the thing rather than receive it. "Compete on price. They can't just charge whatever." He looked at the graph again. "So the Fed squeezes borrowing, and the inflation line comes down that cliff. Fourteen point eight in March 1980, under 3 percent by 1983."

"Sharp increases," Clara said. "That's the word she used. Sharp."

The trouble was that she still couldn't say the whole chain without feeling a gap in it, a link she was asserting rather than seeing. She had two teachers in her head about it: her father, who had lived through it as a kid and called the man at the Fed a hero without ever saying why, and a podcast she'd found where the host spent forty minutes on how much unemployment the sharp rates had cost, in towns she'd never heard of, in years before she was born. Both of them were describing the same graph. She believed both of them and could not make them into one sentence.

"Here's what I'll say tomorrow," she told Theo. "The fact, the numbers, the direction. And then, if she asks why it worked, I'll say the mechanism and then say I'm not sure the cost was worth it, and that I don't know how you'd even measure that." Theo laughed and said Mrs. Okafor would give her a B for honesty, and Clara said she'd take it.

The pitcher was nearly empty. She poured the last of it into two cups, set one in front of Theo without a word, and started taking down the sign while the light went long and orange over the Drapers' roof. "Tomorrow morning," she said, "you quiz me on the walk in. March 1980 first."

"Under 3 percent by '83," Theo said, and raised the cup.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Frozen food can be thawed safely in the refrigerator, in cold water or in the microwave, but not by leaving it out on the counter.
story:
Victor's mother had taken the night shift at the hospital, which meant that for six days the kitchen belonged to him, and the fridge door held a single handwritten schedule that was supposed to make this survivable. Sunday: chicken and rice. Monday: pasta with the leftover chicken. Tuesday: the chili he'd frozen two weeks ago in a container now frosted over like a small glacier. She had labeled everything, which he found both touching and slightly insulting, as though he might confuse chili for yogurt.

The plan was real, though, and the plan was the point. She'd left him money, a list, and one instruction delivered at the door with her coat half on: cook in batches, eat in batches, don't live on vending machine food like your uncle did his first year of college. Victor had a whole year before college, but his mother planned the way other people worried, far in advance and in bulk.

He did the shopping on Saturday with the list open on his phone, and it went mostly well until the store put cilantro next to parsley with no sign, a decision he felt was a trap laid specifically for him. He bought both, because he couldn't admit to the cashier he didn't know which was which, and at home he smelled them side by side until one seemed more like the taco he had in his head. He chose the sharper one. He would find out later, from the internet, that he had been right, and he would feel an amount of pride out of proportion to the achievement.

Sunday he cooked the chicken and rice in one enormous pan, portioned it into containers, and stood in the kitchen feeling like a person who had outsmarted the week. This was the appeal of batch cooking, he decided. Not the food itself but the fact of it, the way planning turned the future into something already half handled. He caught himself wanting to introspect on this, to sit down and examine what it meant about control and adulthood, and then decided against it, mostly because the rice was sticking.

Monday went fine. Tuesday he woke late, opened the freezer for the chili, and stood there while the realization assembled itself. The schedule said to move it to the fridge the night before. He had not done this. The chili was a solid brick, and it was eleven hours until dinner, and he had school in twenty minutes.

His first instinct was the obvious one: leave it on the counter. Everyone's family left things on the counter. His grandmother thawed whole turkeys on the counter overnight, and nobody had ever died. But his mother had said something once, in the car, half-distracted, and he'd filed it away the way he filed things he suspected he'd need later. He couldn't retrieve it whole. Something about the counter being wrong. Something about there being other ways.

At school, between third and fourth period, he looked it up on his phone behind his binder. The answer was blunt. Frozen food could be thawed safely in the refrigerator, in cold water, or in the microwave, but not by leaving it out on the counter. Three options, one prohibition. He read it twice. His grandmother's turkeys floated up in his mind and were quietly escorted out.

The fridge method was out; that took too long, and the chili needed to be dinner tonight. Cold water he considered seriously: the chili in a sealed bag, submerged in the sink, water changed every so often, the way he'd seen described. It had a certain patience to it, an old-fashioned competence. The microwave was faster but felt like surrender, the culinary equivalent of an apology text. He sat with the choice through lunch, and Dylan, across the table, asked him why he was staring at his sandwich like it owed him money.

"Trying to decide how to thaw chili," Victor said.

"Straight to the microwave, obviously."

"You can't just leave it out?" Dylan said, when Victor shook his head. "That's what my whole family does."

"That's what my whole family does too," Victor said. "Apparently we're all wrong."

He went home and did the cold water method, mostly because he wanted to see if it worked, and partly, he admitted, because he liked the image of himself kneeling at the sink like someone from an earlier century, turning a bag of chili in a basin like panning for gold in some alluvial rush of leftovers. He texted his mother a photo of the setup. She replied with a single thumbs up, which in their family constituted a standing ovation.

The chili came out of the bag at six still cold in the middle, and he finished it in the microwave anyway, which meant that in the end he'd used two of the three safe methods, and he felt something almost like respect for the third, the refrigerator one, sitting there in the schedule all along like the correct answer he'd copied down and then ignored. He ate the chili at the counter, alone, and it was good, and he updated the schedule on the fridge so that Wednesday's note now read, in his own handwriting, "move Thursday to fridge TONIGHT, idiot." Then he set his alarm for nine so he could text his grandmother about the turkeys, gently, the way you conduct a plebiscite you already know the outcome of. The phone buzzed first. It was his mother, from the hospital, asking whether he'd remembered to move Thursday down. He got up and opened the freezer.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation.
story:
The test was on Monday, and Sara had brought the textbook to her grandmother's beach house partly to study and partly as a kind of insurance, a proof to herself that the weekend was not only a weekend. She spread her notes on the picnic table under the porch awning, where the wind couldn't take them, and weighted the corners with shells. Behind her the tide came in with its long patient noise, and her cousin Theo was already waxing his board on the sand, though the light was going flat and gray.

He wanted to catch the last hour before dark, and he wanted her to come watch, which was really a way of wanting her to say yes to something. Sara had said maybe, which everyone knew meant she was working. The chapter was on the atmosphere, and she had copied a graph of carbon dioxide across the last century onto a fresh sheet of paper, the line climbing in small annual zigzags like a staircase drawn by someone with a shaking hand. She could describe the line. What she could not yet do, under her breath in the way she practiced for tests, was explain the part underneath it, the part about why the climb meant anything at all.

She started anyway, alone, because that was the method: say it wrong out loud until it stopped being wrong. "Air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen," she said to the shells, "so the gases doing the trapping must be the ones there's the most of." It had a certain logic to it. The most abundant thing should have the most effect, the way the biggest person on a rope pulls hardest. She wrote it down as if committing to it, and the graphite felt decisive against the paper, and for about a minute she was almost satisfied.

Then Theo came up the porch steps dripping, towel around his neck, and read over her shoulder in the way cousins do, without asking. "That's backwards," he said. She bristled at the tone before she registered the words, because he was two years older and had a way of sounding like a textbook himself. "It's not backwards," she said. "It's abundant. It's reasonable." He was already flipping to the page in the chapter, one wet thumb holding his place, and he turned the book toward her so the paragraph faced her and then, unhelpfully, stood there waiting.

She read it twice. Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air, and they are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation. The most common gases in the air were exactly the ones that did nothing. It was like learning that the ocean's water was not what got you wet, only the things dissolved in it. She looked at her own sentence on the page, the wrong one, in her own handwriting, and felt the specific embarrassment of having been confidently wrong in front of a witness. "Okay," she said. "Say it back to me."

"No," Theo said. "You say it." He sat down on the table's edge, letting the towel hang, and the physiology of surfing was evidently exhausting enough that he was willing to postpone it: his shoulders were red, salt dried white on his forearms, and he had the loose contented posture of someone whose own want had already been partly satisfied by the water. Sara said it slowly. Molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation, so nitrogen and oxygen, most of the air, pass heat straight through, the way glass passes light. She paused at that, because it was her own addition, a picture and not a fact, and she wasn't sure yet whether pictures helped her or fooled her. Theo shrugged, which she took as permission.

She went back to the graph. The zigzag line climbed, and now she understood the climb differently, as the accumulated effect of the thin part, the trace gases, the ones that did absorb. She thought about her uncle, who rented out the beach house and had once tried to explain to her what it meant to indemnify the place against storm damage, to make the owners whole after a loss. The thin gases were something like that in reverse, she thought, a small fraction of the whole arrangement holding the entire heat account, so that a small change in them was not a small change at all. She wrote that down too, then crossed out the comparison, because it was the kind of thing that might fall apart if the teacher asked one more question about it. She kept the fact and let the picture go, mostly.

The honest part, which she admitted only to the margin of her notes, was that she still couldn't say why two identical atoms made a molecule that ignored infrared, only that they did. The textbook drew a boundary around her understanding and she could see the boundary clearly, which she decided was better than not seeing it. Some of what she'd learn in college, maybe, sat on the other side of lines like that.

Out on the water the last surfers were coming in, dark shapes against the graying swell, and Theo stood, pulling the towel off his neck. "One more hour," he said. "Come down and sit on the sand with the book. You can practice at me." She looked at the notes, at the graph with its stubborn ascending line, at the crossed-out uncle and his insurance, and then she closed the cover over everything and picked it up. "Quiz me on the walk," she said, and followed him down the steps, the pages clamped under her arm, the sand already impermeable under her sneakers where the tide had gone over it and withdrawn.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
The restaurant on Delancey had laminated menus and a waitress who had already filled Rebecca's water glass twice, which Rebecca took as a signal to stop nursing it and actually order. Across the table, Marisol was folding a napkin into smaller and smaller squares, the way she did when she was deciding whether to be patient.

"Read it again," Marisol said. "Out loud, whole paragraph, no stopping to apologize."

Rebecca flattened the newspaper between the salt shaker and the edge of the plate. The article was short, three paragraphs from a Spanish-language daily about a proposed amnesty for families who had crossed the border years ago, and her summer tutor had assigned it with a note: prepare a spoken summary, in Spanish, by Friday. Friday was tomorrow. Marisol had agreed to help over dinner because Rebecca had helped her move a couch up four flights in June, and because, as Marisol put it, guilt was a renewable resource.

The second paragraph went better than the first until Rebecca hit the phrase "según el ministro." She stopped. In her head, the sentence assembled itself as fact: the minister says, therefore it is, therefore she would repeat it as though the newspaper had verified it. She had done exactly that in high school, she remembered now, in eleventh grade, standing at the front of her English class confidently reporting that a school policy would change because "the article said so," and Mr. Halvorsen asking, gently, which article, and who wrote it, and whether she had checked. She had not checked. She had wanted the sentence to be finished more than she had wanted it to be true.

"Según," Marisol said, when Rebecca asked. She tapped the word with one finger. "It means according to. According to the minister."

"So it's his claim. The paper isn't saying it's true."

"Spanish writers use it all the time," Marisol said, and shrugged, as if to say the sky is blue. "It tells you the statement comes from a source, not from the reporter."

Rebecca sat back. The distinction felt almost embarrassingly small, one small word doing one small job, and yet her whole summary depended on it. If she said the policy would protect ten thousand families, she would be passing off a promise as a fact. If she said the minister claims the policy would protect them, she would be honest but slower, clunkier, and her grade rested partly on fluency, on sounding sure.

"Here's my problem," she said, moving the salt shaker out of her line of sight as if it were a distracting audience. "The summary has to be short. If I hedge everything, I sound like I don't trust my own reading. If I assert everything, I'm lying by accident."

"Welcome to journalism," Marisol said. "Also to dinner." The waitress arrived with two plates of arroz con pollo, looked at the newspaper draped over the ketchup, and moved it to the next table with the resigned efficiency of someone who had seen stranger study sessions.

Rebecca ate with one hand and wrote with the other. For the third paragraph, about destitute families waiting outside government offices, the writer made no attribution at all, and this time Rebecca caught it: the reporter had seen them, or was willing to stand behind the description, and that was different. She underlined nothing, because it wasn't a school text, it was Marisol's paper, and Marisol was watching her with something that had shifted from patience to interest.

"You know you just did the thing," Marisol said.

"What thing?"

"You historicized it. You stopped treating the article like it fell out of the sky and started asking who said what and why now. My professor would give you a sticker."

"I'm eighteen, not five."

"Stickers are ageless," Marisol said. "Now, summary, out loud, in Spanish, and if you say the minister's numbers like they're Gospel I'm taking your rice."

Rebecca breathed, and began. She got through the first two sentences cleanly: the government proposed an amnesty, the minister, según el ministro, claimed it would protect thousands of families. The hedge cost her only one extra word, and her voice did not wobble the way she'd feared. On the last sentence she slowed, chose each verb, and finished with the description of the families outside the offices, saying it plainly, the way the paper had, and then stopped because there was nothing left.

"So," Marisol said, "was it true? What the minister said?"

"I don't know. That's kind of the point. I can tell you exactly who's claiming what, and I can't tell you what's true, and I used to think those were the same failure." Rebecca picked up her fork again. "Ask me something easier. Ask me if this rice is real."

Marisol pushed half her own plate across the table. "Según me," she said, "it's the best thing on this block."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Countering is when one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, keeping both visible to the audience.
story:
The cafeteria at Westfield Regional had been divided by folding tables into a hundred small territories, and Andrew had claimed the corner by the vending machines as his stage. His one-act, which the drama club would perform in three weeks, had been rehearsing in stolen rooms ever since the school auditorium flooded, and today the stolen room was here, between his rounds in Lincoln-Douglas debate. He had taped a rectangle of hallway carpet with painter's tape and set his three actors inside it: Priya, Marcus, and Elise, who was eating Goldfish crackers out of the box because she had forgotten lunch.

"From the top of page four," Andrew said, and walked backward out of the rectangle to watch from where the audience would be, which was a mop sink.

The scene began. Priya delivered her monologue by the taped edge that stood for the window, and Marcus, playing her brother, crossed toward her to deliver his rebuttal. The moment he moved, his shoulder settled directly in front of her face. For the rest of the exchange Priya argued with a sliver of cheekbone visible past his jacket. Andrew stopped them twice, moved Marcus a foot further upstage, and twice he drifted back, drawn by the pull of facing his scene partner, until the problem returned like a debt.

He had prepared for this the way he prepared for debate, with a flowchart of the affirmative case. He understood clashes, he understood positioning, he understood that you won a round by knowing where you stood relative to your opponent. But the stage was not cooperating with his diagrams. In debate, only one of them was trying to be seen; here both of them had to be visible at once, and the rules of that were written in a language he did not speak.

His own round was called over the loudspeaker before he solved it. He debated a girl from Halloway on the resolution about whether civil disobedience in a democracy was justified, and during cross-examination he found himself thinking about Marcus's shoulder, about the geometry of two bodies in a rectangle, and he caught himself and apologized and asked her to repeat the question. When she asked whether jury nullification counted as disobedience, he said that depended on your theory of jurisprudence, whether law lived in the courtroom or in the street, and the exchange exhilarated him so completely that he forgot his timer went thirty seconds over. He won the round anyway.

He came back to the cafeteria carrying a stagecraft book he had found on the abandoned scorers' table, someone's prop or someone's homework, its cover soft with age, its glossary talking about footlights and obsolescent rigging. He turned to the diagrams of stage movement, and there it was, a pair of arrows: an actor crosses, the other actor shifts position to balance the stage, keeping both visible to the audience. He read the entry three times, standing in the mop-sink audience, while Priya and Marcus ran lines around him.

"Try it again," he said. "Marcus, cross when you say 'you never listen.' Priya, when he moves, take two steps downstage and turn out. Just feel for it." They ran it. Marcus crossed, Priya shifted, and suddenly there were two faces in the rectangle instead of one and a half, and the stage felt balanced, weighted correctly, like a good round felt before the rebuttals began.

"What's that called, when I move like that?" Priya asked, wiping her hands on her jeans.

"Countering," Andrew said.

Elise, who had been quiet for an hour, looked up from her crackers. "I thought directing was just telling people where to stand," she said. "This is more like arguing. You're always responding to what the other person does." Andrew had assumed, when the club made him director because he was organized, that the job was about control, about imposing a plan; now he understood it as something closer to cross-examination, listening and adjusting, and he said so, and Elise nodded slowly and then said she wanted to try the counter move too, in the last scene, where she had been standing frozen by the door. He had blocked her there weeks ago and never questioned it, and he changed his mind out loud, in front of all of them, and moved the tape.

They ran the whole play once, the four of them in the folding-table territory, and when Priya countered Marcus perfectly in the final scene, the Goldfish box still open on the floor beside Elise's mark, Andrew clapped once, loud, and then made them do it again.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The electric field between charged plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate, the direction a positive charge would be pushed.
story:
The park's floodlights wouldn't come on until six, and Elizabeth's quiz was at eight the next morning, so she was doing homework on the flat bottom of the bowl with her back against the concrete, physics book open on her knees, her board flat beside her like a retired pet. She had come to skate. She had told herself she would skate for an hour, then study. Two hours later the book was still open to the same page and her wheels were still cold.

Dex came off the mini ramp and dropped onto the concrete beside her, breathing hard, holding his phone like something he had just rescued from a fire. "Sunset's at 5:51," he said. "The contest wants the video by midnight. If I don't land a clean kickflip in natural light I'm not entering."

"So land it."

"So watch me not land it." He leaned over her book, dripping. "What is that?"

"Physics. Two charged plates. You have to figure out the field between them." She turned the book so he could see the diagram, two parallel lines crowded with arrows, and beside it her notebook where she had copied the arrows going the other way, bottom to top, because she had been half watching Dex and half guessing.

"Which one's right?" Dex asked. He had his own problems, but he was seventeen and constitutionally incapable of passing a question unanswered, even someone else's.

"Mine, probably." She said it fast, the way you say things you haven't checked.

Down the ramp, Rosa slid to a stop and walked over, board under her arm, peering at the two diagrams with the frank skepticism she applied to everything, a jaundiced view of all studying done anywhere but a desk. Rosa was a year ahead, pre-med track, the kind of person who titrated her coffee by the milliliter until it was exactly drinkable. She tapped Elizabeth's notebook. "Which plate is positive?"

"The top one," Elizabeth said. "In the book's version."

"Then here's what I want to know. If I put a proton in the middle, which way does it go?"

Elizabeth opened her mouth to say up, because up was where she had drawn the arrows, because up had felt right when she drew them. She closed her mouth. Somewhere in the blur of the chapter there was a sentence she had read four times without taking in, and now it assembled itself: the field points the way a positive charge would be pushed. She looked at the top plate, positive, and imagined the proton there between the plates, and the proton being positive would be pushed away from it, toward the negative plate, downward, and so the field between the plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate.

"Down," she said slowly. "The proton goes down. From positive toward negative. My arrows are backwards."

"So the book's right and you're wrong," Rosa said, not unkindly.

"Mine are backwards." Elizabeth crossed out her arrows with three hard strokes, and the strange thing was that crossing them out felt better than being right would have. She had wanted the answer. She had ended up with the reason, which was heavier and better, like the difference between being handed a board and building one.

"5:40," Dex said. He stood, rolled his ankle once against the concrete, and picked up his board, an ancient thing with a graphic worn to a ghost, practically antiquity, older than both of them. He pushed off toward the mini ramp while Elizabeth drew fresh arrows, all of them downward, from positive to negative, checking each one against the sentence she now couldn't unlearn. Rosa watched her, then the ramp, then her phone.

He must have tried the kickflip eight times. On the ninth the board flipped cleanly under him and he caught it in the air, rolling away down the far side, and Elizabeth and Rosa both shouted, and Rosa's phone was already up and recording when the floodlights banged on all at once, flooding the park with flat white, drowning the last of the natural light, and the contest rules, Dex yelled from the bottom of the ramp, still rolling, plainly requiring daylight, said nothing about lamps.

"Take it anyway," Elizabeth called.

"Take two," Rosa said, still recording. Elizabeth turned back to her notebook, drew one more arrow, downward, and wrote under it, in small letters, which way a proton would go, and then, because the lights were on and the quiz wasn't until morning, she finally stood up and stepped onto her board.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: William Appleman Williams's 1959 book The Tragedy of American Diplomacy began the revisionist school, arguing that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War.
story:
The box in his grandfather's study was labeled GARDEN BOOKS, and Victor only opened it because he was avoiding his college reading list, which sat on the desk upstairs like a dare. Inside, under seed catalogs and a moth-eaten guide to pruning roses, he found a slim blue hardcover, its spine cracked white. The Tragedy of American Diplomacy, William Appleman Williams, 1959. He knew the name from somewhere. He sat cross-legged on the floor and read the first chapter while dust drifted in the window light.

By the time his grandfather shuffled in with two glasses of lemonade, Victor had a pencil in his teeth and a frown he could feel in his forehead. "Grandpa, this guy is an American historian blaming the United States for the Cold War."

"He was a Wisconsin man," his grandfather said, handing him a glass. "I heard him talk once, in sixty-one. Hall full of crew cuts and nobody clapped." He lowered himself into the desk chair. "Started a whole argument. They called it the revisionist school."

"Revisionist." Victor turned the word over. In his AP class the Cold War had been a clean machine: containment, the Iron Curtain, the Soviets closing off Eastern Europe, the United States responding. Mr. Ruiz had called the Soviet Union an expansionist power that had to be checked. Victor had written that in an essay and gotten an A. Now here was Williams arguing that American economic expansion helped cause the whole thing, that the drive for open markets pushed Washington into confrontation.

He said as much, haltingly, and his grandfather only shrugged. "I'm a retired mailman, not a historian. But I lived through it. Everybody had an explanation and everybody was sure."

Victor spent the afternoon in the study with Williams on one side of the desk and his textbook on the other, a confounder at the heart of the whole business: he liked both accounts, and liking both felt like a kind of cheating. The textbook's story was tidy and moral, the free world resisting a system meant to subjugate it. Williams made the United States an actor with its own interests rather than a passive defender, and that rang true too, in a way that unsettled him. He copied passages onto index cards. He spread them across the carpet like a dealer laying out a hand.

"Supper in twenty minutes," his grandmother called from the kitchen, where something with onions had been going soft and sweet since four o'clock.

"In a minute," he said, and did not move.

At supper he interrogated his grandfather between passes of the mashed potatoes. Did people in 1950 really believe the Soviets would attack? "Some did, some profited from saying so," his grandfather said, sawing at his pork chop. Victor pushed further: did the Marshall Plan look like generosity or like a market grab from the inside? His grandmother laughed and said Victor had gone to college a month early. His grandfather chewed for a while. "From where I stood, it looked like both. You could hold two things, last I checked."

Afterward, in the study, under the lamp with its green glass shade, Victor tried to hold two things and found his hands full. The evidence Williams leaned on was real enough, the open-door language in American documents, the pressure for access to foreign markets. The textbook's evidence was real too, the tanks, the sealed borders, the speeches in Moscow. The trouble was that both stories fit the same facts, the way two keys can seem to fit one lock. Whichever he believed depended on what he brought to it, and he could feel that about himself, which was worse than being wrong.

He thought about Mr. Ruiz, who had taught the orthodox version with such certainty that certainty itself had seemed like knowledge. Victor had trusted the tone. He wrote at the bottom of his last index card: the tone is not the evidence.

His grandfather appeared in the doorway, toothbrush in his shirt pocket. "Figured anything out?"

"Some," Victor said. "The revisionist argument's tenable, more than I wanted it to be. But it doesn't prove the other one false. I don't know yet which one explains more, or whether that's even the right question." He gathered the index cards into a stack and squared the edges against the desk. "I'm taking the book to school."

"It's yours," his grandfather said. "It's been sitting in a box for forty years. Books don't mind waiting, but they shouldn't have to."

Victor slid the blue hardcover into his backpack, between the textbook and his notebook, where the two accounts would ride pressed together all the way back to his room. He zipped the pack shut and left the lamp burning a moment longer, looking at the empty space in the box where the book had been.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Spike tape is coloured tape used to mark where furniture and actors should be placed on the stage floor.
story:
The black box theatre smelled of dust and old paint, and the light grid above it hung like a sky someone had strung with cheap stars. Alexandra had been assigned the one-act in September, three weeks before the festival, and for the first week she had mostly stood at the table of scripts and said things like "maybe try it warmer." The actors nodded and did exactly what they had done before. On Friday, Marcus moved the sofa.

He did it for a practical reason, or at least a plausible one. His character had to storm to the door, and the sofa sat in his path, so each night it migrated a foot closer to the wings until it was practically riparian, sitting at the edge of the stage like a town settled on a riverbank. Nobody mentioned it. The actors adapted around the drift, and the geography of the scene quietly changed, so that the argument that was supposed to happen across the room happened side by side, like two people on a bus.

Alexandra noticed this on Tuesday and could not decide whether it mattered. Part of her thought the scene had actually improved; the proximity made the quarrel feel crammed and claustrophobic, which suited it. Another part of her remembered reading the playwright's notes, that the distance between them was the point. She had been trying for two weeks to hold both of those ideas, the written intention and the accident of the room, without letting either one flatten the other, and she was beginning to suspect that directing was mostly this: metabolizing every small accidental discovery into something deliberate, or deciding it wasn't worth digesting at all.

What she wanted, concretely, was a rehearsal where she stopped reacting and started deciding. She had watched Mr. Halloway run the fall musical from the back of the house, calling out corrections in a voice that never rose, and she had also watched Devi, the senior who had directed last year, sit on the floor with the actors and let them argue until the scene found itself. Alexandra had assumed she had to choose between them, the general and the collaborator. On Tuesday night, staring at the drifted sofa, she began to think the choice was false, and that the problem was not style but tools. She didn't have the tools yet to say what she wanted with any authority, so she said "maybe" instead of "there," and "warmer" instead of anything a body could do.

On Wednesday she came in early, before Marcus, before anyone, carrying a roll of fluorescent pink tape she had found in the props cabinet under a collapsed sombrero. She had overheard the stage crew use the phrase once, months ago, when a set piece for the musical had gone missing in transit across the boards, and she had looked it up that night at her desk, hunched over her phone while her mother watched cooking shows downstairs. Now she knelt and tore off short lengths and laid them on the floor: here for the sofa's front legs, here for its back.

Priya arrived first, coffee in hand, and stood at the edge of the stage looking down. "What's that?"

"Spike tape," Alexandra said. "It marks where things go. Furniture. Actors too, if you want."

"You're spiking my sofa."

"I'm spiking everybody's sofa."

When Marcus came in and reached for the armrest out of habit, Alexandra was standing by the table, and she said, "Sofa stays on the pink tonight. If it still doesn't work there, we'll talk, but I need to see the scene with the room the way we planned it." Her voice did not rise. Marcus looked at her for a second, shrugged, and slid the sofa back onto its marks with a scrape that made the empty theatre ring.

The scene that followed was worse and better. Worse because the long quarrel across the distance felt thin at first, shouted rather than lived, and Priya kept cheating toward Marcus as if the room were pulling them together. Better because Alexandra could finally see the problem as a problem. She called a halt, walked onto the stage, and placed Priya on her own small square of tape, downstage left, facing a quarter turn out. "You're not listening to him from here," she said. "You're deciding whether to." Priya ran the moment again and something happened in her face that had not happened in a week of warmer.

Afterward, while the actors gathered their bags and argued about whether the ending needed a laugh, Alexandra stayed behind to sweep. She looked at the pink marks glowing faintly under the work lights, the sofa settled on its island like it had grown there. She still did not know if the distance was right, or only dutiful; she suspected she would not know until an audience sat in those folding chairs and breathed with it. But the room meant something now, and she had made it mean that. She folded the tape roll closed, set it on the props table next to the sombrero, and snapped off the work lights one by one, leaving the pink to hold its places in the dark.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Aristotle named three means of persuasion: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, the logic of the argument.
story:
The debate topic was printed on the syllabus in French, and Annabelle had taped it to her grandmother's kitchen window so she would see it every time she filled the kettle: "Les énergies renouvelables doivent remplacer complètement le charbon d'ici 2050." Five minutes, entirely in French, no notes. The argument in favor was the side she'd drawn, and for three days she had filled a notebook with statistics, in French, on grid capacity and installation costs, until the margins of her pages looked like a stock ticker.

Her grandmother's house smelled of lavender and old paper, the smell of a place that had acclimated to the same occupants for forty years and had stopped changing for anyone. Grand-mère moved through it without looking, setting down a cup of coffee beside Annabelle's notebook and sliding the sugar bowl closer, because she remembered that Annabelle took sugar even when she said she didn't. "Tu travailles toute la matinée," she said, not as a question, and pulled a chair to the table without waiting for an answer.

Annabelle had come here because her own house was loud and her grandmother's was not, and because Grand-mère was the only person she knew who would sit through five minutes of shaky French without laughing. She smoothed the notebook flat. "Je peux pratiquer?" she asked, and when her grandmother nodded and folded her hands, Annabelle began, reading in her head and speaking aloud: coal plants release this much carbon per year, solar costs have fallen by this much, other countries had done this by that date. Numbers, dates, comparisons. She made it two minutes before she lost the word for "subsidy" and stopped, hands cold around the cup.

"You have convinced a machine," her grandmother said in English, which she did only when something mattered. "Not a person."

Annabelle frowned. "It's a debate. Facts are the argument."

Grand-mère didn't answer that. She got up, went to the hallway shelf where the dictionaries lived next to her late husband's engineering manuals, and took down a battered paperback, its spine held with tape. She set it in front of Annabelle and tapped the cover once, then went back to washing dishes, leaving her alone with it.

It was a translation of Aristotle, her grandfather's, from a college course. Annabelle turned pages with one finger, picking out what she could, and found a passage marked in pencil so faint it was almost gone. She read the Greek words, then the English glosses beside them in her grandfather's handwriting. "Ethos," she said slowly, to the kitchen more than to anyone. "Pathos. Logos." Her grandmother turned off the tap and looked over. "Ethos, c'est la crédibilité du locuteur," she said, drying her hands, and then, pointing at the page in order: "Pathos, les émotions du public. Logos, la logique de l'argument." Three means of persuasion, the old author said, and Annabelle sat back and looked at her notebook as if seeing it for the first time. Every line she had written was logos. Pure, stacked, airless logos. Nobody in that classroom would be moved by grid capacity figures recited in her second language, because all they would hear, all they could hear, was a sixteen-year-old reading numbers she had copied down.

She thought about what she actually believed, which was the part she'd skipped. Her grandmother's village in the mountains had lost its coal jobs before Annabelle was born, and Grand-mère never talked about it except once, in the garden, saying the town had gone quiet the way a house goes quiet. That was pathos, or something near it, but using her grandmother's loss as an emotional prop felt like taking something that wasn't hers. And ethos, her own credibility, was close to nothing; she was a student who had never seen a coal plant. She chewed the end of her pen and wrote, in English, in the margin where the French couldn't reach: what right do I have to say this, and what would make them believe I mean it?

The honest answer was that she could speak from what she knew. She had watched the turbines go up on the ridge past her school; she had heard her uncle, who installed them, call the job a sinecure compared with the refinery work he'd done at her age, safe and indoor and dull. He'd said it half as a complaint. So the transition wasn't clean, wasn't only a graph sloping upward; it was a trade, and she could say that, in French, if she learned the words for it. She looked up "incertain" in the dictionary and wrote it at the top of a fresh page, then built backward from it. Not a bellicose speech, all attack, the kind her teammate Marcus gave, jabbing the air with statistics like a fencer. Something slower.

She practiced twice more that afternoon. The second time, when she stumbled on the word for "worker," her grandmother said it for her without turning from the stove, and then said it again, syllable by syllable, until Annabelle's mouth got it right. It was nearly five o'clock, the winter light going amber on the window and the taped topic card, when Annabelle stood up and gave the whole thing, five minutes, no notes, ending on the ridge with the turbines and the quiet her grandmother had described, not borrowed but acknowledged, attributed to her in French as the person who had told it to her. Her voice shook somewhere in the middle and steadied.

When she finished, the kitchen was quiet. Her grandmother dried her hands slowly, and Annabelle waited, not knowing yet whether it had worked, whether the uncertainty she'd admitted at the end was honesty or weakness, whether a debate you couldn't finish was still a debate. Grand-mère came around the table and straightened the topic card on the window, smoothing the tape with her thumb.

"Encore une fois," she said, and sat down.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, a ball dropped from a table and a ball launched horizontally from the same height hit a level floor at the same time.
story:
Vanessa had until eight the next morning, when her father would drive her to the regional campus for the physics placement exam, and the practice test on her bed still had four blank problems. The sixth one asked for the range of a ball launched horizontally off a cliff, and she had read it so many times the words had stopped meaning anything. She sat cross-legged on the carpet with her calculator, a borrowed textbook, and her phone propped against a stack of laundry.

Marcus texted at nine. He was in her physics class and had failed the same placement exam last year, which was how he'd ended up in remedial fall semester. He wanted to study together, but at his house, which was a fifteen-minute walk, and he wanted to bring Priya, who was already through the material and mostly came to argue.
