Vanessa said fine, come here instead, my dad's asleep by ten and we have the kitchen table.

They arrived at nine thirty with a bag of chips and a marble. Priya put the marble on the table like it was evidence. "Marcus thinks the problem set is out to get him," she said. Marcus said the problem set was out to get him, specifically. He had a disincentive to believe otherwise, since he had already paid for the retake.

They worked the first three problems at the kitchen table, trading the calculator back and forth. Vanessa kept splitting the numbers wrong. She wanted to treat the ball's speed as one thing, one arrow, and the formulas kept asking her for two things instead. "You dichotomize it," Priya said, drawing a right angle in the margin. "Horizontal is horizontal, vertical is vertical, they don't talk to each other." Vanessa copied the angle into her own notebook but didn't feel it click. It looked like two problems stapled together, and she didn't see why nature was obligated to cooperate with the stapling.

Marcus leaned back and spun the marble under his palm. "Okay, but here's my question," he said. "If I roll this off the table, and Priya just drops hers from the same height at the same second, which one hits first." Priya said the dropped one, obviously, it has less distance to travel. Marcus said no, the rolled one, because it's going faster. Then he said ten dollars on it. Priya looked at Vanessa, and Vanessa, who had no idea and needed one before morning, said they should actually do it.

The table was seventy-one centimeters high, Vanessa measured it twice. The floor in the kitchen was tile, which mattered, because they needed to hear the hits. Priya took both marbles, stood on a chair to keep her hands level with the tabletop edge, and made Marcus sit on the floor with his eyes closed and his ear near the tile, since he'd insisted sound was more reliable than sight and neither of the girls trusted their own reflexes. Vanessa stood by the light switch with her phone timer she knew she'd never need, only to feel official.

The first try was no good because Priya's fingers moved at slightly different times and Marcus said he'd heard two clicks and refused to say which came first, taking the position that ambiguity favored his bet. They argued about it. On the second try Priya released the dropped marble a half-second late on purpose, to test whether Marcus could actually tell, and he could, which made them trust him more. On the third try she flicked the launched marble hard, and on the fourth she barely nudged it, and both times Marcus, eyes shut, said one sound. "I hear one sound, like both at once, like it's one click with an echo in it." Priya made him repeat it for the phone recording. One click, marble rolled, one click, marble nudged. Same single sound, every time.

Vanessa went back to her notebook while they were still arguing about the ten dollars, which Priya now wanted to declare void and Marcus now wanted to win on a technicality. She looked at her right angle, at the two columns she'd drawn, horizontal on one side and vertical on the other. The marble that was rolled and the marble that just fell had hit at the same time, every time, and the rolled one had been going fast sideways when it did, and that hadn't mattered at all to when it landed. So the sideways part of the motion and the falling part really were separate, the way Priya's right angle said, and she could fill in one column without touching the other. She worked problem six straight through, from the given speed and height down to a range in meters, and then problem seven, and the numbers came out clean both times.

Marcus was dour about losing, in the way he got when the universe sided with a textbook, and he paid Priya in quarters from the jar by the fridge. Vanessa watched them count, and she understood the experiment now, and she also understood that she couldn't have said why the two marbles hit together, only that they did, and that this was enough to solve everything on the practice test even if it wasn't enough to satisfy her. She wrote a question mark in the margin next to her right angle, next to the two clean answers, and left it there. Priya scooped the marbles off the floor and put them back in the bag with the chips. "Again at seven," she said. "Bring the quarters."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995; its lead designer was James Gosling.
story:
Anna arrived at the coding club twelve minutes late with her laptop under one arm and a lie already prepared about the bus. In fact she had stood outside the door for most of those twelve minutes, listening to the clatter of keyboards through the window, deciding whether she was the kind of person who went in. She told herself she was. She was still telling herself when Mr. Okonkwo's student assistant, Priya, opened the door and said, "You're Anna, right? You can sit anywhere that isn't the broken chair."

The room had been a chemistry lab before the school commandeered it for the club, and the periodic table was still bolted above the whiteboard, which someone had half-erased to make room for the words "ENCAPSULATION" and "GETTERS." Anna took the seat farthest from the broken chair, which happened to be next to a boy named Dmitri who was already typing. On the projector, Mr. Okonkwo had written a fragment of Java in blue marker: a class called Book, with a private field for a title.

"Private means only the class itself can touch it," Mr. Okonkwo said, which was the last full sentence he offered before turning everyone loose, because his theory of teaching was that hands learned faster than ears. Anna's theory, inherited from her mother, a nurse who read instructions twice before opening any box, was the opposite. She sat with the empty file open and wanted the explanation first, the whole architecture of it, before she committed a single brace to the page.

She typed nothing for six minutes. She had told Priya at sign-up that she'd done "some programming," which was true in the way that having visited a beach is having swum. She had finished half of an online course two summers ago and abandoned it at the chapter on loops. What she had not abandoned was the reason she'd started: her grandmother's recipe notebook, three decades of handwritten kugel and borscht in a script only Anna could still decipher, slowly mildewing in a drawer. She wanted to put it somewhere it couldn't rot. She had imagined, in the abstract, that this would involve programming. She had not imagined a room full of people who already seemed to know what they were doing.

"You're staring at it like it owes you money," Dmitri said, not unkindly.

"It kind of does."

"Start with the fields," he said. "Then write the getters. Getter is just the word for a method that hands the value back to whoever asks."

She wrote the Book class the way she did everything, twice as slowly as necessary, and privately narrated to herself that she was being careful rather than afraid. This narration was a habit of hers, and it was not fully honest. When the class compiled on the first try, she felt a jolt of something disproportionate, a feeling she would later refuse to describe as joy in front of anyone.

Then came the test. Mr. Okonkwo wanted a main method that constructed a Book, called the getter, and printed the result. Anna wrote the constructor call, ran it, and got a compiler error shaped like an insult: cannot find symbol. She read it four times. Her instinct, inherited from the same careful mother, was to assume she had broken something fundamental, that the error was a verdict on her rather than on the code. Dmitri leaned over without asking, which she resented for exactly two seconds before his perspicacity proved him right: she had named the class Book and saved the file as book.java.

"Case matters," he said. "Everything matters. That's kind of the whole deal with this language."

"Whose idea was that?" she asked, half furious.

Dmitri shrugged. "Some Canadian guy. James Gosling designed it." He typed something, pulled up a page on his phone. "Sun Microsystems released it in 1995."

She stared at the number. "That's older than us."

"By a lot," said Priya from across the room, where she was helping a younger student who had, at a robotics competition the previous weekend, announced to her whole team that Java was basically new, invented for their generation, and been corrected by a judge. Priya still found this funny. Anna did not find it funny; she found it vertiginous. She had assumed she was arriving early to something, that the tools were being forged roughly in step with her need for them. Instead the language predated her by years, had been used by strangers for purposes she would never know, and the notebook in the drawer was decaying on a timeline that had nothing to do with whether she caught up.

She fixed the filename, and the test ran, and the title of the book, which she had made "Recipes, 1987," printed cleanly to the console. It was a small output. She looked at it for a long time.

Here were the two things she was holding, and she could not yet make them one: the caution that wanted to understand before touching, and the evidence, fresh on her screen, that touching was how understanding arrived. Her mother's way had kept recipes legible for thirty years and had also kept them in a drawer. Dmitri's way broke things constantly and fixed them in seconds. She did not think either was simply right. She thought, provisionally, that the error message had taught her more than the explanation had, and that this was possibly true and possibly unfair to explanations, and she could not yet say which.

"Again?" Dmitri asked, meaning another class, another test. He was already writing the skeleton on the whiteboard: Recipe, it said, with a blank where the fields went.

Anna saved her file first, twice, under two names, because some habits she was keeping. Then she pulled the laptop toward her and wrote, in the blank, "private String ingredient."

"What's the getter for that?" Dmitri asked.

"You already know," she said. "You're testing me."

"I'm testing whether you'll say it."

"getIngredient," she said. "Lowercase i."

He capped the marker and stood back, and on the whiteboard above his handwriting the ghost of the periodic table looked down on all of it, every element still in its fixed and ancient place.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void.
story:
Sienna's laptop sat open on her grandmother's kitchen table between a bowl of tomatoes and a jar of pens, and on the screen was a deadline: the assignment was due at eleven, and her test kept printing zero. "It's a constructor," she said to the room, because saying things out loud had started to help. "It's supposed to run when I make the object. It just doesn't."

Her grandfather was shelling peas at the counter with the unhurried rhythm of a man whose whole day was diurnal in a way hers never was, sunrise for the garden, radio at noon, lights out before ten. He had programmed once, decades ago, assembly on machines the size of the stove, but when she asked him about Java he only shrugged and said the languages had changed more than the peas had. He came and stood behind her anyway, drying his hands on a towel.

"Show me what a failing test looks like," he said.

She showed him. She had built a small class called Book, its fields marked private so nothing outside could reach in and change them, and a getter method called getTitle to hand the title back out. In her test she wrote a line that constructed a Book with the title Persuasion, then asked for the title and printed it. The screen said null. Not Persuasion, not an error, just null, as though the book had arrived in the world with nothing written on it.

"That's the strange part," Sienna said. "It compiles. Everything runs. It just acts like my code for setting the title isn't there at all." She leaned back and turned her pencil over, the way she did when a problem had stopped being annoying and become interesting. She had two habits of mind that had always pulled against each other. From her mother she had the instinct to tinker: change something, run it, see what happens, change it again. From her father she had the instinct to introspect, to sit quietly and read every line until it confessed. For a week she had been toggling between them, and neither had won.

"Read it to me," her grandfather said. "Slow. Like you're reading me a recipe."

She did. "Public class Book. Private string title. Public void Book, string t, open brace, title equals t, close brace." She kept going, but something snagged, and she stopped with her finger on the screen. The constructor was supposed to share its name with the class, and it did, Book and Book. But it was not supposed to give anything back. It was not even supposed to say void. Hers said void. She had typed it the first day, copying the shape of every other method she knew, because in Java everything gave something back, even if what it gave back was nothing.

"Wait," she said. She deleted four letters. Just that. She ran the test again, half certain the screen would shrug at her the same way, and the console printed Persuasion, plain and certain as a page. She laughed, one short note, and her grandfather tapped the counter twice with two fingers, which she understood to be applause.

"Four letters," he said.

"Four letters and I lost three days." She was already writing another test, then a third, checking that the private fields really were closed off, that the getters really handed back what the constructor put in. She thought about the argument she'd been carrying on with herself all week, the tinkerer versus the reader, and decided it had been a travesty of a debate, because the answer was both: you tinker until the machine shows you where to read, and then you read until the line confesses. Though she had to be honest with herself about what she still didn't know. Why the language was built so that one small word could make a whole method silently become something else, she could not have said. Maybe there was a reason. Maybe it was just an old door that locked if you leaned on it wrong. She wrote the question in the margin of her notebook, the way her grandmother wrote tomato varieties on the cellar jars, to be opened later.

At ten minutes to eleven she submitted, closed the laptop, and carried the jar of pens to the drawer where they belonged. Her grandfather had finished the peas. Outside, the moths were already at the porch light, keeping their own hours.

"How many did you shell?" she asked.

"Enough for two dinners," he said, and slid the bowl toward her so she could carry it in.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
story:
The pharmacy smelled of floor cleaner and Halloween candy going stale, and Connor stood at the counter with a box of adhesive bandages he didn't need, buying time. His brother Sam was outside on the curb, seventeen and hunched, and the walk-in clinic two blocks over stopped taking patients at four o'clock. It was twenty past three. Their mother had extracted a promise from Connor before her shift, the way she inculcated everything, by repetition until it felt like his own idea: take him, don't lecture him, come back with the truth instead of something off a forum.

Connor had rehearsed on the bus. Consent first, because that was the part Sam would roll his eyes at and need anyway: it's ongoing, it can be taken back, silence isn't a yes. Then the clinic part, which was easier, because facts about appointments were boring enough to be believable. What he had fumbled was contraception, because Connor had absorbed his own education in fragments, from a gym teacher who'd clearly wanted to be elsewhere and from classmates who spoke with false authority. He had told Sam, on the bus, that if his girlfriend got on the pill they'd be covered. Sam had nodded like a man accepting a map.

Ahead of him at the counter was a girl in a university hoodie, sliding a white paper bag across the glass. "Quick question," she said to the pharmacist. "This, the birth control. Does it protect against infections too? Like, everything?"

The pharmacist, a small woman with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair, didn't sigh, though Connor sensed she'd answered this a hundred times. "No, it doesn't," she said. "It prevents pregnancy. Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections." She tapped the bag. "Keep taking it as prescribed. They're not either or, a lot of people use both."

The girl thanked her twice, cheeks pink, and threaded past Connor toward the door. He stood there recalibrating, the map in his head suddenly wrong in a way that mattered. He'd told Sam covered. He'd said it with the confidence of someone who wanted the conversation over. Behind him the pharmacist called a name that wasn't his, and an old man shuffled up with a cane and a prescription for blood pressure, and Connor stepped to the side with his useless bandages and thought, quickly, about what he actually knew.

"Excuse me," he said, when the old man had paid. "That thing you said. About condoms. Is that in writing anywhere, like a pamphlet?" She looked at him, at his age, at the way he glanced through the window at the curb, and something in her expression softened.

"Someone out there waiting?"

"My brother. I'm taking him to the clinic before four. There's a girl. He's scared, I'm the ride and apparently the encyclopedia." His laugh came out thinner than he intended. "I already told him something wrong today."

She disappeared into the rack behind her and came back with two pamphlets, one on testing, one on methods, and a card for the clinic's Tuesday hours. "You're doing more than most rides do," she said. "Tell him testing is routine there, nobody gives a speech. They ask questions, they draw blood or give you a cup, you're out in forty minutes." She paused, ringing up the bandages anyway. "And telling him you got something wrong? That's the part he'll remember. It gives him permission not to know things either."

Outside, the light had gone the pale gold of late October, and Sam sat with his elbows on his knees, radiating a melancholic patience, as if he'd already decided the afternoon would happen to him rather than be chosen. Connor sat down on the concrete beside him rather than stand over him, which felt like its own small correct decision, arrived at by volition instead of instinct.

"So I got something backwards on the bus," Connor said, and handed him the pamphlet. "The pill, if Mia goes on it, that's pregnancy only. Condoms are actually the only common contraceptive that also lowers your infection risk. The pharmacist said it, not me, she said it like it was a sentence she says every day." Sam turned the pamphlet over, read a line, turned it back. "And the clinic's open till four, so we have to go now, and the testing part is blood and a cup and about forty minutes, and I'll be in the waiting room the whole time unless you'd rather I wasn't."

Sam was quiet for a moment, watching a pigeon investigate a candy wrapper. "Forty minutes," he said.

"Forty minutes," Connor said, and stood, and held out his hand for no reason other than that his brother looked like a person who needed one.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate.
story:
Sophie spread the case packet across the wide table by the window, where the riparian willows along Miller Creek hung so low their branches tapped the glass whenever the wind came up. She had been assigned the impossible half of the assignment: to argue both sides of a school dress-code case before a mock court, five minutes for the students, five minutes for the administrators, as though she were two people who despised each other and also, somehow, the same person. Her partner Marcus wanted the student side only. He had decided, sometime in September, that a college recruiter was coming to the mock trial regional and that only a rousing defense of the oppressed would be memorable, and he had not revised this theory since.

"Start with the students," he said, tapping the packet. "Judges love the underdog. I'll do the closing, you do the opening, we crush them in the middle."

"I have to argue the school's side too. That's the whole assignment. Both sides."

"That's a waste of your best material." He slid a printout toward her, a summary of some case he'd found at midnight, badly cited, the margins full of his own capital letters. She pushed it back and opened the library catalog instead, because the packet's only clue was a footnote: the students' lawyers had leaned on a famous Supreme Court case from the sixties, one that every student-speech argument since had leaned on too.

She typed "Tinker" and the catalog gave her nothing, then "student speech" and gave her a shelf number she couldn't interpolate into any aisle she knew, until the map on the wall revealed that constitutional law lived in a section she had walked past a hundred times on her way to the fiction. She went and got the volume herself, a fat blue book with a cracked spine, and carried it back with both hands.

"Here," she said. She read it twice before she said it out loud. "Tinker v. Des Moines. Nineteen sixty-nine. The Court ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate."

Marcus sat up. "Say the last part again."

"Students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate."

"Schoolhouse gate," he repeated, savoring it. "That's the line. That's the line they'll remember. Seven to two, that's not even close." He copied it onto his notepad, forming each word as if it might smudge, and Sophie noticed he wrote it under his own name, as though it had occurred to him.

They began running the argument right there, Marcus playing judge with a paperback held like a gavel. Sophie stood and argued that the dress code was a viewpoint restriction, that the school had punished a message and not a distraction, that Tinker stood behind her the whole way. Then she sat, took a breath, stood again as the other Sophie, and argued that a dress code was content-neutral, that schools could regulate conduct that disrupted learning, that the schoolhouse gate was a real boundary with real reasons behind it. She had expected the second speech to feel like lying. Instead it felt like translation, the way she could argue her mother's side of a fight once she'd cooled off. Ms. Perrin had called the method a dialectic, testing an idea against its opposite until something sturdier survived, and Sophie had rolled her eyes at the word in class and now found it was simply what she was doing, out loud, in a library, getting louder.

"Order," Marcus intoned, banging the paperback down. "Counsel will approach the bench." He was grinning, thoroughly enjoying himself, doing voices. A boy at the next table looked up from his chemistry homework. The reference librarian, a small woman named Mrs. Okafor whom Sophie had known since story hour, appeared at the end of the aisle with the unhurried gravity of weather.

"This is a library," she said.

"We're practicing free speech," Marcus said. "It's a Supreme Court case."

"Students do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate," Sophie said, "but I guess we shed them at the library door." Mrs. Okafor considered this, and something in her face suggested she had heard every possible joke about this in thirty years of shelving law books, and chose not to dignify it. She pointed to the study room at the back, glass-walled, soundproof, usually reserved for tutors.

They gathered their papers and followed her. In the study room Sophie laid the blue volume between them, open to the page she'd flagged, and the argument resumed behind glass, safely inaudible to everyone else. She took the student side again and hit the line cleanly, seven to two, the schoolhouse gate, and watched Marcus mouth it along with her, having already made it his.

"Okay," she said finally, checking the time. "One more run-through of the school's side. Then I'm done."

"You're really going to argue against us?" Marcus said. "In front of the recruiter?"

"In front of the judges. And it's not against us. It's the other half of the assignment."

He shook his head, then flipped his notepad to a fresh page and clicked his pen. "Fine. Then I'll be the judges, and I'm going to be ruthless." He set the paperback gavel on the table and squared his shoulders. "Counselor, the Court has heard enough about the schoolhouse gate. Convince me there's such a thing as a gate at all."

Sophie stood up and reached for the blue book.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Blocking is the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals.
story:
Aaron had been told that directing was mostly making decisions, and he had believed this the way you believe in weather: abstractly, until it rains on you. The community theatre had given him a slot on Thursday nights, a one-act called The Letter, set on a steppe, which in rehearsal meant a bare stage with two chairs and a folding table meant to suggest an inn. He had three actors: Priya, who was twenty and patient; Marcus, who was seventeen and pugnacious about line readings; and Dolores, who was sixty and had been in forty-one shows and watched Aaron the way a cat watches a bird that is behaving strangely.

The first Thursday went well, which he later understood to be the trap. They sat around the table and read the script, and Marcus argued that his character should shout in the opening, and Priya argued back, and Aaron let them argue because it sounded like collaboration. The second Thursday they got on their feet, and scene two collapsed. Priya crossed to the window that didn't exist. Marcus, following his instinct toward the table, walked directly into her, and the two of them stood there in the collision like people unsure whose fault a fender bender was. Dolores, from her chair, said nothing, which was somehow louder than Marcus's apology.

He went home and did what he'd done his whole life when lost, which was read. Somewhere past midnight, in a chapter about rehearsal process, he found the word he'd heard older directors use without ever parsing. Blocking. The planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals. He read the sentence twice. It was not a vocabulary word, it was an accusation. The stage was not supposed to organize itself. That was his job, and he had not done it, and so the actors had done what actors do when no one decides: they bumped into each other in scene two.

He wanted to expiate Thursday's disaster before anyone could bring it up, so he arrived early with a box of donuts and a pad of graph paper. Priya took a donut. Marcus took two and said, "So are we going to fix the traffic jam?" Dolores took none, sat down, and folded her hands.

"Blocking," Aaron said. "That's the word. It means where everyone stands and moves. I set it. I should have set it already."

"I know what it means, sweetheart," Dolores said.

He had drawn the stage on the graph paper, a rectangle divided into squares, and he had numbered the positions. Priya starts at the table, center. Marcus enters from the left, crosses downstage right, stops at the second chair. When Dolores, as the innkeeper, comes in, everyone else freezes for a count of three, which gave the entrance weight without anyone having to shout. He walked them through it like a diagram come to life, and it was awkward, it was geometry, Priya kept saying "downstage right?" and pointing hopefully in two directions, but by the third pass the collision was gone, a problem that had seemed like a personality conflict revealed as arithmetic.

But arithmetic was not the whole of it, and that was the part he hadn't expected. When Marcus hit his mark and turned to deliver the letter monologue, the speech that had been the best thing in the table read went flat, because standing exactly where told, he had nowhere to go with the rising line. Aaron watched him try it twice and heard the air go out of it. He could keep the blocking and lose the scene, or he could throw out the blocking and lose the order that had made the scene possible at all. Dolores caught his eye across the stage and raised one eyebrow a fraction of an inch, which he chose to interpret as an invitation.

"Marcus," he said. "Forget the chair. Cross to me while you talk. Priya, hold your spot but turn with him." It worked, or at least it worked better: the monologue had motion in it now, and the motion had meaning, because Marcus was moving toward a person instead of toward furniture. Aaron wrote the change into the graph paper and understood that the paper was not a rulebook. It was a record of decisions, and decisions could be re-made, and both things were true: the director set the movement, and the movement only lived if it answered something the actors actually felt in the moment. He could not have said where the line was between those two. He drew it in pencil.

On Sunday night Priya sent him a message about the fourth Thursday, which she would miss for a college interview.

"That's fine," he wrote back. "We'll run the first two scenes and I'll take your lines from the table." He pressed send before thinking, then sat looking at the little delivered check. Priya replied with a single line of laughter and then: "You're going to read the innkeeper's daughter. A boy playing her." He typed and deleted three answers before settling on the true one: "I'll stand where you stand and read flat, so Marcus can practice the turns. It's just blocking with my body in it."

Thursday came. Dolores watched from her chair with the folding script in her lap while Aaron stood on Priya's mark, holding his sides flat and lifeless, and Marcus crossed toward him and said the letter speech, and it was strange, it was the best the speech had ever been, and Dolores stood up at the end of it and walked slowly to the edge of the stage. "Do that again," she said. "Exactly that. Don't touch anything."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain.
story:
The textbook had been open to the same page for forty minutes when Samantha's brother pushed the kitchen door open with his foot, carrying a shoebox under one arm. "Mom said you have to help me with my project," Danny said, setting the box on the table beside her flashcards. He was fourteen and had learned exactly how to make a request sound like a sentence being handed down.

"I have a bio exam at eight tomorrow morning," Samantha said.

"You're doing bio. I'm doing bio. It's efficient." He lifted the lid of the shoebox. Inside were beads he had scavenged from a broken necklace, paper clips, and an index card covered in his handwriting, which even upside down looked like it was apologizing for itself. "I have to explain how DNA makes a protein by Friday. I don't get it at all."

Samantha looked at the card. He had copied the words transcription and translation from somewhere without any punctuation between them, as if they were one long thing that had happened to him. She thought about refusing. She thought about the exam, about the sixty terms she had not yet mastered, and then she thought about how explaining something was the only reliable way to find out whether she understood it, which was a piece of sophistry she could live with, since it happened to also be true.

"Fine. Sit down. But you're going to do the work." She slid the textbook across to him and pointed at the diagram she had been staring at, the one with the DNA ladder unzipping, a single stranded copy peeling off it. "Start here. Tell me what you see."

"That the big rope split and made a smaller rope."

"Which is called what?"

He squinted at the caption. "Messenger RNA. It's like a copy of one half."

"Okay." She took his index card and drew a quick sketch, the messenger RNA as a long dotted line. "Now here's where I always got it backwards, so listen and tell me if I'm wrong. The copy goes out of the nucleus to this gray blob. The blob reads it three letters at a time and picks up the matching bead." She held up one of his necklace beads, then a paper clip. "It's like threading beads on a string while reading the pattern. You move along the pattern, add a bead, move, add a bead."

"That's the ribosome," Danny said, tapping the gray blob before she could. "It's on my card."

"It is the ribosome." She frowned at her own sketch, because something about it had snagged, some wrongness she could feel before she could name it. She had written in her notes that the ribosome built the chain by gluing the beads, and gluing felt wrong, too craft-store, too vague for something this precise. She opened her laptop and typed a fragment of her notes into the search bar, then read silently for a moment. "It joins them with peptide bonds," she said. "That's the actual word. The ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins the amino acids together with peptide bonds to build the protein chain." She made herself say it once more, slower, the way she would say it tomorrow under exam conditions.

"So the beads are the amino acids," Danny said. "And the string is the protein."

"The string is the chain that becomes the protein." She stopped. She had been about to adjudicate the distinction out of existence because it was easier, and instead she drew the chain curling into a folded lump at the end of the line. "It's a chain until it folds. Then it's a protein."

Danny started threading beads. He read letters off the messenger RNA sketch she had drawn, three at a time, and picked beads by a color code he invented as he went, and twice he lost his place and had to back up, and once he threaded a bead that didn't match and Samantha made him pull it off. "The ribosome doesn't get to make mistakes like this," she said. "Or it does, and there's a whole other chapter about it that I am not learning tonight."

"So what do you actually get wrong on the exam?" he asked, not looking up.

She thought about lying to seem more in command of the kitchen table. "Direction," she said. "Which end it starts from, which way the ribosome crawls. I'll get it right tomorrow because you made me say it out loud four times." He looked up at that, pleased, and she waved him back to his beads. "Keep going. You have eleven left."

Outside, the streetlight buzzed on, and the rain that had been threatening all afternoon finally arrived, drumming the window in a low, lugubrious rhythm that would have suited her mood an hour ago but now just sounded like weather. Danny threaded the last bead and held up the finished string, slightly crooked, a paper clip at each end where the knots should have been.

"That's a protein," he said.

"That's a protein," Samantha said, and reached over and folded it, once, into the shape of something small and alive.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In transcription, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA, which carries the gene's instructions.
story:
The kitchen smelled of burnt coffee and engine oil, because Uncle Ray had been in the garage since seven and Dad had left the pot on the warmer until it scalded. Isaac spread his notes across the table, three pages of diagrams copied so many times the ink had gone gray, and tried to read them while his cousin Junie swung her legs against the chair and watched.

"Is that homework?" Junie asked. She was eleven, dumped on the house every morning that week while her mother covered shifts at the clinic, and she had decided that Isaac, home from his first summer after starting college, was the most available entertainment in the county.

"It's for a test. I have to retake it Monday." He said it flatly, the way you say a thing so nobody asks the next question. But Junie was eleven, and eleven-year-olds ask every next question.

"What'd you get wrong?"

"A whole section." He turned the page so she couldn't see the circled grade at the top, red ink pressed hard enough to emboss the paper. His father's laptop sat at the other end of the table, an obsolescent thing with a fan that wheezed like the tractor, and Dad had been on furlough from the plant since May, which meant the laptop stayed home now, which meant Isaac studied at the kitchen table instead of the library, which meant Junie. Everything connected to everything, which was, inconveniently, the subject of the test.

Junie leaned over his diagrams, uninvited. "What are those circles?"

"Cells. And inside them, DNA." He tapped the twisting ladder he'd drawn. "You know DNA. Everybody says DNA."

"It's like the thing that makes you you."

"Sort of. It's more like instructions. The whole book of instructions for building you, sitting in one room, and the building happens way out in another room." He pointed to a second shape he'd drawn, a little blob labeled with cramped letters. "The problem is, the book never leaves the room."

Junie frowned at the drawing. "Then how does anybody read it?"

Isaac opened his mouth, and then realized he was about to say the exact sentence that had cost him twelve points in May. He'd written something vague about the gene "traveling" to the cell's factories, and the grader's red pen had circled it and written see me. He had gone. He had sat in the office while the professor explained, and he had understood it in that moment so completely that he'd been almost embarrassed, and then he'd gone home and let it blur again.

"Okay," he said slowly, dragging a fresh page toward him. "Say it's the farm. Say your breeding records, the good ones, the whole binder with every bloodline in it, lives in the house. You wouldn't take the binder out to the barn, right? Grease, rain, a calf steps on it. It's the only copy."

"Dad photocopies pages," Junie said. "Like when he sells a heifer, he copies her page for the buyer."

Isaac stopped. The kitchen was quiet except for the laptop's fan and the distant clank of Uncle Ray's wrench. "Yeah," he said. "He does."

He drew the binder, then a single sheet coming off it. "That's what the cell does. The instructions stay inside, in the DNA. But the cell makes a working copy and sends that out. A single page, one gene, good enough to work from." He pointed to the copy in his drawing. "It's called messenger RNA."

"Who makes the copy?"

"There's an enzyme, RNA polymerase. It reads one strand of the DNA, and builds a matching strand of that RNA, and that strand carries the gene's instructions out to where the protein gets built." As he said it, he drew the enzyme crawling along the ladder, the new strand peeling off behind it, and he could see now why the protein-making machinery out in the cell didn't need the original at all. The messenger carried everything. The binder stayed home on its shelf.

"Like the photocopy," Junie said, satisfied, and went back to her swinging.

Isaac copied the whole pathway onto a clean sheet, transcription, then the reading of the messenger into amino acids, then the folding of the protein, and he thought about the professor's office and his father's idle summer and how a mistake in the copying gets carried out into everything built from it. He worked until the coffee smell turned to evening.

From the garage came the sound of the wrench going still, and then his father's boots on the steps. Isaac covered the graded page with his elbow without deciding to.

"Still at it?" his father asked, stopping in the doorway, wiping his hands.

"Monday," Isaac said.

His father looked at the table for a long moment, the diagrams, the fresh copy, the covered paper under Isaac's arm. "Want me to quiz you after supper?"

"Sure," Isaac said, and slid the graded page into his notebook, spine down, before he answered anything else.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people.
story:
The assignment went up on the whiteboard on Monday: a ten-minute play, drawn from a moment in your own life, staged in class on Friday. Amelia wrote the deadline in her planner and underlined it twice, then opened her notebook and started listing everything that had happened to her last summer, which was the summer her parents sold the house on Delancey Street and moved the family across town before her senior year.

Her first draft had six scenes. Scene one, the kitchen, where her mother announced the move. Scene two, the realtor's office. Scene three, the new bedroom, empty except for boxes. Scene four, the old house the day of the sale, scene five the goodbye party at the park, scene six the first morning in the new school district, which technically was September but she folded it in anyway. She typed it all Tuesday night, and it came to forty-one pages.

On Wednesday, Mr. Okafor walked the rows during work time and stopped at her laptop. He scrolled, then looked at the clock on the wall. "How long is this?" "Forty-one pages." He did not lecture her. He said only, "What do you know about how a ten-minute play is built?" and moved on to Devon's desk, which meant she was on her own to find out.

At lunch she sat with Priya in the library and searched on the school's slow desktops. The first result repeated the same sentence on three different sites: a ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people. She read it aloud to Priya, twice. "Few characters," Priya said, counting on her fingers. "You have your mom, your dad, the realtor, three friends from the party, a neighbor. That's eight." "One setting," Amelia said. "I have six." She copied the sentence into her notebook and closed the laptop.

The problem was that the summer felt true only as a whole. Compressing it felt like a kind of lie, like she was impugning the significance of the party or the empty bedroom by cutting them. Priya argued the opposite: that the draft as written would rush every scene, and rushing was its own lie. "Pick the one where you actually changed," she said. Amelia pushed back that change happened in the gaps between scenes, in the drives across town, and Priya said, "Then put the drive in the play, but you can't put everything in the play." They were quiet for a minute, and Priya added that Amelia was treating memory like some fragile thing when really it was ductile, it bent and held its shape. Amelia said that was exactly what worried her.

That night she made two lists. On the left, the moments she could stage in one room with two, maybe three people: the kitchen announcement; the last dinner in the old house; the phone call with her grandmother, who refused to come see the new place. On the right, everything that would have to be implied rather than shown. She noticed that the phone call, which she had not even written in the draft, was the moment she remembered most exactly: her grandmother's voice going flat, then the long silence Amelia had filled by describing the new kitchen as if she were reading a city ordinance, clause by clause, to someone who had no intention of obeying it.

Thursday she cut the play down to nine pages. One setting, the new kitchen, boxes still taped. Two characters, Amelia and her grandmother's voice on a phone propped against a stack of dishes. She read it out loud in her bedroom with a timer and it ran eleven minutes, so she cut the opening monologue, and it ran nine minutes forty. The last line belonged to the grandmother: "Send me a picture, then. When the walls are painted."

Friday, third period, the desks were pushed back against the lockers. Devon went first, then Marisol, whose play was one girl talking to a mirror for the whole ten minutes, which the class called pretentious until the final line, and then nobody called it anything. When Amelia's turn came, she stood by the taped-square kitchen while Priya, off in the corner by the windows, read the grandmother's lines in a lowered voice. Somewhere in the fourth minute, Amelia stopped performing and started listening to the silences she had written, and found that they held. When Priya said the last line, the room stayed quiet a moment longer than it needed to, and then Mr. Okafor, from the back, said only, "Four minutes for notes," and clicked his pen.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Air resistance slows real projectiles, so a thrown ball usually lands shorter than the calculation that ignores air resistance predicts.
story:
The launcher was a two-by-four with a nail, a spoon, and a bungee cord, and by four o'clock on Saturday it had already cost Thomas most of his afternoon and one gutter panel. The regional engineering fair was Sunday at noon. His sister Wren sat on the back steps with a clipboard she had appointed herself to, tallying where each ball actually landed against the chalk circle he had drawn on the lawn, twenty-two feet from the firing line.

"Shot nineteen," she called. "Short again. Nineteen feet four inches."

Thomas crouched over his notebook, where the calculation was written out for the fifth time, clean enough now that no judge could accuse him of fudging. He had worked the physics the way Mr. Okonkwo taught it: the ball left the launcher at a known speed, at a known angle, and then you split that launch into two separate pieces. The horizontal part stayed constant, the ball cruising sideways at the same rate the whole flight. The vertical part was the one gravity got to touch, dragging it down with a steady acceleration, and the time the ball spent in the air came entirely from that vertical half. Once he had the time, the horizontal half told him the distance. It was a beautiful trick, cutting one motion into two easy ones, and it predicted twenty-two feet exactly. His chalk circle sat at twenty-two feet exactly. The ball, nineteen times out of nineteen, disagreed.

"That's half a foot of margin of error," Wren said, chewing the clip of her pen. "Isn't the whole point of physics that it's supposed to work?"

He had wondered that himself, walking the tape measure back and forth across the grass until the numbers in his head stopped matching the numbers in his book. The calculation wasn't wrong, he was nearly sure of that. He had checked the angle with a phone app, timed the bungee's pull with a stopwatch, done the arithmetic twice. What he couldn't check was the air. The idea had arrived sometime around shot eleven, uninvited: the calculation treated the air as if it weren't there, and the air, all around his backyard in its warm October invisibility, quite obviously was.

"It's like the problem lives in a vacuum," he said, mostly to himself. "The whole formula. Gravity and nothing else."

Wren looked at him the way she looked at most of his sentences, with affectionate suspicion. "You sound like Grandpa talking about the church."

That landed harder than she meant it to. Their grandfather had spent forty years as a deacon in a church that ran their town like a small theocracy, everyone's Sunday and most of everyone's conscience, and after his divorce the elders had made him stand up and read a confession he hadn't written. He had expiated that sin for years afterward, or tried to, driving meals to shut-ins, repainting the parsonage fence, serving a verdict he privately considered wrong. Thomas had only understood it recently: his grandfather had accepted that a perfect system said one thing and his life said another, and he had chosen, week after week, to honor the system anyway. Thomas had spent a whole evening in the garage deciding he would not be that kind of person, not exactly, though he loved the old man. He wanted to be the kind who found where the system ended and said so out loud.

He launched shot twenty. Nineteen feet six inches. He walked out and stood in the space between the chalk circle and the flattened grass where the balls actually fell, a gap about the length of his forearm, and looked back at his sister.

"Air resistance," he said. "That's the gap. It slows the ball down, so it lands shorter than the math says. The math isn't broken. It just doesn't know about the air."

"Can you put the air in the math?"

"Not before tomorrow. That's differential equations, like, real engineering. Nobody in my class can do that." He picked up the ball and rolled it in his palm. "But I can aim differently. I can shoot past the target by however much the air takes away, so the ball lands on it."

"So the answer to the perfect theory is to fudge?"

"It's not fudging. It's the theory plus the backyard." He thought of his grandfather again, standing in that gap between what the system promised and what the world delivered, and felt a strange steadiness settle in his chest, the kind that came from holding both things at once. He would tell the judges everything: the calculation, the flaw in the calculation, the correction he had measured himself. He wasn't certain the correction would hold on a different lawn, in different wind. He was certain that claiming otherwise would be a lie, and that the honest version was, in its way, better physics.

The sun had dropped enough that the chalk circle glowed faintly orange. Wren erased her tally sheet, wrote CORRECTION TRIALS at the top, and clicked the pen. "Fire when ready," she said.

Thomas set the ball in the spoon, pulled the bungee back past the angle his notebook said was correct, felt for the angle the backyard said was correct, somewhere between the two, and let go.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Adolphe Thiers's History of the French Revolution, published from 1823 to 1827, praised moderate leaders such as Mirabeau and Lafayette and condemned radicals such as Robespierre.
story:
The exhibit hall was almost empty by four o'clock, which was why Jordan had chosen it. His essay was due at eight the next morning, and he had written nothing except a title and one sentence he had already crossed out. The traveling exhibit on the French Revolution had come to the city museum that month, and his teacher had said, more than once, that the assignment was not about what happened in 1789 but about how people had described it since. A historiographical essay, she kept calling it, and Jordan had nodded each time without knowing what the word asked of him.

He moved past the guillotine blade under glass, past a shoe buckled in the style of the ancien régime, and stopped at a glass case containing books. Behind the glass, leaning open, sat three fat volumes. The label read: Adolphe Thiers, History of the French Revolution, published 1823 to 1827. Jordan recognized the name from somewhere and could not place it, which bothered him the way a word on the tip of the tongue bothers a person, physically, at the back of the jaw.

"You're the fourth person today to stand there," a voice said. A girl about his age was sitting on the bench beside the case, a museum volunteer lanyard around her neck and a paperback open on her knee. "Nobody knows who he is."

"Thiers," Jordan said. "I know him from something."

"He ran France later," she said. "Like, decades after. President, put down the Commune, all of it. But he wrote the history first. That's the weird part, at least I think it's weird. He was a young journalist when he started it." She held up her paperback, which was the exhibit catalog, dog-eared at a chapter called Aftermath and Afterlives. "You can read about it in here if you want. We're not supposed to let people handle the desk copy, but nobody's checking."

Jordan sat down and took the catalog. He read standing facts and then read them again. Thiers praised moderate leaders such as Mirabeau and Lafayette, the catalog said, and condemned radicals such as Robespierre. Jordan copied the sentence into his notebook and then, underneath it, wrote a question that had not been in his head two minutes earlier: what did it mean that the man who wrote the first great account went on to govern? His draft so far, three pages of summary about the Terror, suddenly seemed like a report on a movie rather than anything a reader could think with.

The volunteer, whose name tag said Priya, watched him write. "Is that for school?"

"Due tomorrow. Eight a.m. I was going to write about how the Revolution was good or bad, and now I don't think that's even the assignment."

"It's not, probably," Priya said. "My brother did that essay two years ago and bombed it. He wrote ten pages on Napoleon." She paused. "He really wanted to lionize Napoleon, and the teacher kept saying, whose Napoleon? Napoleon according to whom?"

Jordan laughed, then stopped, because the question had weight to it. He turned back to the catalog. Thiers had loved Mirabeau, a man who could work a room and then betray it; Thiers had hated Robespierre, a man who could not be bought. And thirty years after publishing those volumes, Thiers had signed off on shooting Parisians in the streets. Jordan did not know yet what to do with that sequence, but he could feel the shape of it, the way a fact stops being a fact and becomes an argument somebody once needed.

"Here's my problem," he said out loud, mostly to himself. "If I write about Thiers, I'm just taking one more person's side. His version. I'd be doing the same thing he did, only fifty times later."

"So say that," Priya said. She shrugged. "My brother's teacher also wrote on his paper, the strongest essays admitted what they couldn't settle."

Jordan looked at the clock above the exit. The museum closed at five, and his bus took forty minutes. He had one sentence in his notebook and a due date at eight, and somewhere between here and his desk he would have to decide whether Thiers belonged in the essay as evidence or as a warning. On a blank page he wrote, "Every history of the Revolution is also a history of the person writing it," and then sat looking at the line, testing whether he believed it or only admired its sound, its cheap verisimilitude of wisdom.

The overhead speakers announced closing in fifteen minutes. Priya stood, tucked the catalog under her arm, and nodded at the glass case with the three volumes inside it. "He built this whole grandiose reputation on those books," she said. "Then he got actual power, and people remembered the shootings longer than the chapters."

Jordan closed his notebook, zipped it into his bag, and walked back to the case one more time. The open volume showed an engraving of Robespierre, thin-faced, drawn with all the warmth of a wanted poster. Jordan photographed it, checked that the image was sharp, and headed for the exit while the guards began roping off the hall behind him.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution in his 1863 book on drama technique.
story:
Liam sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with a legal pad, a pencil he had chewed to splinters, and a deadline: by Sunday he had to stage a ten-minute play about a moment from his own life, in front of everyone at the summer drama workshop. The carpet still smelled faintly of the orange soda his cousin had spilled at Thanksgiving. He had chosen that Thanksgiving as his subject, the fight his uncle and his mother had had over the cranberry sauce, of all things, which had ended with his uncle walking to his car in the rain and nobody speaking for a year. It was good material. He knew it was good material. The problem was that on the page it lay there like a dropped sandwich.

"What's the pyramid for?" his sister Priya asked, flopping onto the couch above him with her own homework.

He turned the legal pad around. He had drawn a lopsided triangle, sliced it into floors, and labeled them from bottom to top: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution. "It's from this German guy. Gustav Freytag. He wrote a book on drama technique in 1863, and he described dramatic structure as a pyramid. I found it in one of the workshop books." He tapped the narrow top floor. "I'm trying to figure out where my climax goes."

"Your what goes where?"

"The climax. The peak. The whole sauce fight builds to it." He stared at the little box. "Except when I write it, the fight just sort of happens, and then there's a lot of falling action where people eat quietly, and it goes on forever."

"Maybe the sauce isn't the climax," Priya said, and returned to her biology notes with the air of someone who had said everything she intended to say.

Liam considered this the way he considered most of Priya's remarks, which was reluctantly and then completely. If the sauce wasn't the peak, what was? He climbed the pyramid in his head, floor by floor. The exposition was easy: the table, the relatives, the rain starting outside. The rising action was his uncle arriving late, his mother saying something small and sharp about it. But the top of the pyramid, the point where everything turned, might not be the shouting. It might be the moment after, when his uncle stood in the doorway with his coat half on, and his mother said, "Take some pie," and nobody could tell whether it was kindness or surrender, least of all the two of them.

That was the scene. He wrote it three times, and each time it got shorter, which felt wrong and then felt right. On the couch, Priya watched him cross out half a page.

"You look debilitated," she said. "It's a vocab word. It means wiped out."

"I know what it means. I'm not debilitated. I'm concentrating." He was, in fact, a little debilitated. He lay back on the carpet and addressed the ceiling, where a water stain shaped vaguely like a statesman glared down at him like a misanthrope who had been forced to attend a party.

From where Priya sat, her brother looked like a marionette someone had dropped, limbs everywhere, pencil still in hand. She watched him mutter to the stain on the ceiling, something about falling action, something about how Thanksgiving had a whole year of falling action afterward and maybe that was the actual play. She had assumed his workshop was all costumes and showing off. She hadn't expected him to take it seriously, and she hadn't expected the seriousness to look like this, like arguing with the ceiling about his uncle.

"Can I read it?" she asked.

"It's not done."

"It doesn't have to be done. I'm not the workshop."

He handed the pad up to her and listened while she read, which was mostly a matter of listening to her not laugh at the wrong places. She did laugh at their grandmother's line about the gravy boat, which he had taken directly from life, and she went quiet at the doorway scene, the pie line, the coat half on.

"You should make Uncle Ray come to this," she said, handing it back. "Not Mom. Just him."

"He'd hate it. He'd say we were being dramatic."

"You are dramatic. It's a drama workshop. It would be parochial of you to only think about how Mom sees it." She paused. "That's another vocab word. It means narrow. Like only caring about your own little patch of things."

"I know what it means." He took the pad back. She was right, though, and he hated how often she was right about things she delivered like fortune cookies. He had written his mother's version of the doorway because he had stood behind his mother that night. His uncle had been a shape in the rain, and then a silence, and then a year of not asking. He could not climb inside that shape. He could only put it on a stage and let it stand there with its coat half on, and let whoever was watching decide what the pie meant.

On Sunday morning he moved the coffee table against the wall, roped Priya and two neighbors into playing relatives, and marked the doorway with masking tape on the carpet. When the boy playing his uncle paused at the tape, coat half on, and his neighbor Suzie delivered the pie line into the quiet, Liam stood in the dark corner by the bookshelf and did not breathe. Somewhere out past the tape was the falling action, and past that the resolution, and he still did not know what belonged in that last narrow floor. The lights came up. Suzie set the pie down on the table and looked at the door.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Mishnah lists 39 categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath, which the rabbis linked to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle.
story:
Connor had been at his grandfather's apartment for two hours, and the argument had not moved since the first minute. His cousin Micah kept glancing at his phone on the counter, the screen dark, and their grandfather kept glancing at it too, though he said nothing. Finally Connor said what everyone was circling around. "So is turning it on breaking Shabbat, or not?"

Micah picked the phone up, then set it down. "It's not like lighting a fire. You tap glass."

"You don't know that it's not like lighting a fire," their grandfather said. "You don't know what any of it is, actually." This was unfair, and also true in a way Connor resented, because he didn't know either. He had come for the weekend to look at colleges and had expected brisket and cable, not a jurisdictional dispute over a Samsung.

"The whole thing's arbitrary," Micah said. "Rabbis just made up rules. Like, who decided electricity counts as work?"

Their grandfather went to the shelf and took down a thick volume, cloth-covered, its spine cracked pale at one place. "You want to prognosticate about what rabbis decided," he said, handing it to Connor and not Micah, "or you want to read what they wrote?" Connor took it because it was handed to him, and because Micah was already halfway into the fridge.

The book was a Mishnah, the index told him that much, and Micah's question had a real answer in it, which surprised him. There was a chapter on Shabbat, and inside that chapter a list. Thirty-nine categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath. Not a loose impression of forbidden things but an enumerated catalogue, like a building code. He read down it: sowing, plowing, kneading, baking, weaving, spinning, dyeing, sewing, tearing, hunting, slaughtering, kindling, extinguishing, striking a hammer. He was still reading when Micah leaned over his shoulder with a plate of turkey.

"Striking a hammer," Micah said. "So it's about construction. Big deal."

"It is a big deal," Connor said, and then he found the part that stopped him. A commentary in smaller type explained that the rabbis derived the list from the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle. He sat back. "The Tabernacle," he said aloud, testing it. The list wasn't arbitrary in the way Micah meant by arbitrary. It had a logic: the portable sanctuary the Israelites carried in the desert, the work of making it, and a day on which that work stopped. The rule came out of a text, out of a story about tents and dye vats and hammered metal. He did not think this settled the phone question. He thought it changed what kind of question it was.

Here it is worth saying what Connor could not yet have said, but what he was beginning to feel his way toward. He had walked in thinking the argument was between old superstition and obvious modern sense. Now it looked more like two languages being spoken at a kitchen table, and the interpreter was absent. The rabbis had taken a principle, rest on the seventh day, and given it edges; the edges were drawn from the world they knew, which was not a world of glass and capacitors. The question of the phone was whether the edges were the principle or only its clothing. He understood that a person could honor the principle and shed the clothing. He understood that another person could hold that the edges were what kept the principle from evaporating entirely, that a rule with no edges was a mood. He did not know which person he was.

"So can I turn it on or not?" Micah asked.

"You're asking the wrong guy," Connor said. "I'm asking the same thing."

Their grandfather had gone quiet in a way that Connor, glancing up, recognized as attention. The old man had expected the book to be a rebuke, and instead his grandson was reading it like a puzzle, and something in his posture had softened, as though he had prepared an argument and now had no one to argue against.

"Grandpa," Connor said. "The fire category. When they say kindling, is that about making something, or about the heat?" Because if the phone produced heat in its circuits, even a little, one could argue it fell inside an old category by the text's own reasoning; and if the category was about the act of transformation, fire changing things, then a phone was something else entirely, and a rabbi would have to decide whether tapping glass transformed anything. He was not trying to win now. He was trying to see the shape of the problem the way the people who built it had seen it.

His grandfather pulled out a chair and sat down across from him. "That," he said, "is a better question than your cousin's." Micah made a noise into his turkey but did not dispute it. Connor turned back to the page, ran his finger down the list of thirty-nine again, and stopped at kindling.

"Okay," he said. "Show me the Hebrew."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it; the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience.
story:
The auditorium smelled like dust and the ghost of a hundred assemblies, and Kaitlyn stood on the stage with a binder she had labeled, in a moment of optimism, DIRECTOR. Inside were fourteen pages of blocking notes, a photocopied script of the one-act, and a cashbox ledger for the disbursement of her tiny budget, which so far consisted of eleven dollars for gaff tape and four for a bag of pretzels. She had volunteered to direct because no one else had, and because she had assumed that directing mostly meant knowing what you wanted. She was learning, in the flat afternoon light, that it mostly meant knowing how to make other people want it too.

"Move upstage," she said, and Marcus, who played the landlord, took a step toward the edge of the stage, toward the front row of empty seats, toward her.

"No, up," she said. "Away."

"Up is away?" Marcus said. "Who decided that?"

"That's not the point," Kaitlyn said, though it was beginning to seem like the point. The whole afternoon was dissolving into it. Priya, who played the daughter, had her own theory, which was that upstage meant the important place, the raised place, and so she kept drifting toward the back wall as if proximity to the cyclorama conferred status. Marcus kept drifting down toward the audience because, he said, that was where the faces would be. They were, in blocking terms, two tectonic plates moving in opposite directions, and Kaitlyn was the fault line.

She tried metaphors. She tried sketching arrows in the script margins, tiny vectors that looked, she admitted, like a diagram of something going wrong. She tried the thing her debate coach called desensitizing the audience to your authority, which in practice meant saying a firm thing several times until it stopped sounding firm. Nothing worked. Priya finally sat down on an upturned crate and said, "If we don't know why it's called that, we're just memorizing nonsense syllables. I can't move on nonsense syllables." She said it kindly, which somehow made it worse.

What Priya could not have known was that sitting in the fourth row was Mr. Okonkwo, the retired postman who built sets for the community theatre and had come to measure the stage for their flats. He had been quiet for an hour, the way carpenters are quiet, and now he spoke without looking up from his tape measure. "Why is the back called up?" he asked. "Every flat stage I've worked on, the back is level with the front. Somebody at the theatre asked me that once and I gave him an answer I made up on the spot." He retracted the tape with a snap. "I'd like the real one."

That question went home with Kaitlyn, folded into her binder between the blocking notes and the ledger. Her younger brother had a theatre book on his shelf, a fat orange paperback someone had given him, and she found the answer on page forty, between two paragraphs about thrust stages. She read it twice, then a third time, feeling the small click of a lock that had never needed a key, only the right one. She wrote it on her hand because she was out of notecards, and she wrote it small, near the wrist, where she wouldn't sweat it off.

From where Priya sat on the crate, watching Kaitlyn come in the next afternoon with something written on her hand, it looked like a girl who had either joined a cult or found a coupon. Kaitlyn called them to the middle of the stage and did not open the binder. "The back of the stage is called upstage because it's away from the audience, and the front is downstage because it's toward them," she said. "The names come from old raked stages, the ones that sloped down toward the audience." Then she paused, because she had rehearsed this part in the shower. "So when I say up, I mean the uphill direction, even though this floor is flat. We're standing on the ghost of a slope."

Marcus walked upstage, then downstage, then turned and did it faster, and Priya saw that something had changed in his body, that the words had become directions instead of riddles. She stood up off the crate. She had spent the previous night deciding she was going to quit, that she would tell Kaitlyn after rehearsal that the one-act was tangential to her actual life, a thing she had let herself be talked into by a girl with a binder. She had even drafted the speech on her phone. She deleted it now, quickly, before it could be entered into evidence, and walked to her first mark.

They ran the whole first scene without stopping, and when it ended Marcus was upstage left exactly where he belonged, and Priya was downstage of him, and the light through the dusty window made a long parallelogram on the boards between them, falling downhill toward the empty seats. Mr. Okonkwo, still measuring, called out, "You're flat, but you're tilted," and Priya laughed, and Kaitlyn made a note in the margin of her script, then crossed it out and wrote it on her hand instead.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In a presidential system, the president is elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term and cannot be removed simply because the legislature disagrees with them.
story:
The committee room at city hall smelled of floor wax and cold coffee, and by four o'clock the youth council had been arguing about the same resolution for over an hour. Nathan had come because his civics teacher had mentioned the council looked good on applications, and he'd stayed because the arguments were better than anything in class. Now the chair was calling a ten-minute break, and Nathan followed Dami and Priya out to the corridor, where the vending machine ate coins and gave back nothing but pretzels.

"You two were both born somewhere else, right?" Priya asked, shaking the machine in a practiced, resigned way. "Nathan, you were?"

"Born here. My mom wasn't." He leaned against the wall beside Dami, who had arrived from Ghana in eighth grade and still carried a bottle of pepper sauce in his backpack for the cafeteria's sake. "Why?"

"Because we're doing that model conference in March," Priya said, "and the theme is different systems of government. Ms. Okafor put me in charge of it, and I don't know anything. Like, actually anything."

Dami fished out his own coins and fed the machine with a touch that seemed to coax it. "In Ghana we have a president," he said. "You vote for him directly. Four years, and he serves his four years even if the whole parliament hates him." The machine surrendered a bottle of water. He passed it to Priya without being asked, because she'd wanted one and had been too proud to say so.

"So they can't just kick him out?" Nathan said.

"Not for disagreeing with him. Not simply because parliament doesn't like him." Dami shrugged. "It's different from Britain, isn't it? Your mother's country." He turned the question gently, the way he did when he already suspected the answer.

Nathan thought of his mother watching the news from London on her laptop at the kitchen table, the volume low so as not to wake his father. He had absorbed the shape of it without ever naming it. "The prime minister isn't elected separately," he said slowly, testing the sentence as he went. "She's just whoever leads the biggest party in Parliament. And if the party turns on her, or Parliament does, she's out. There's no fixed term the way you mean it. She's in office because Parliament keeps her there." He heard himself say it and felt the two systems click against each other in his head, like the halves of something he'd been carrying without knowing.

"So in one you pick the leader directly and he's locked in," Priya said, writing on the back of her agenda, "and in the other the leader is basically made by the legislature and can fall with it."

"Careful," Nathan said. "'Locked in' isn't right either. Dami said he can't be removed just for being disagreed with. That's not the same as never." He paused, aware he was arguing against a simplification he'd offered himself a minute ago. "That's the part I keep getting wrong. I want it to be one clean rule, and it's two clean rules that overlap."

The corridor was emptying as the break ended, fluorescent light pooling on the linoleum. Priya looked at her notes, then at Nathan, then tore the page out and folded it into her pocket instead. "Okay," she said. "I'll just ask people what they know and see what falls out."

Dami laughed. "You're already doing politics."

"Terrible," Priya said. "Also, Nathan, you're on the conference panel now. I put your name down during the last agenda item."

"You put my name down before you asked me?"

"I asked you," she said. "You said 'huh' and nodded. That's consent in committee."

Nathan followed them back toward the room, where the chair was already tapping her pen against the podium and someone had left a half-eaten pretzel on the seat nearest the window. He sat down beside Dami and wrote, in the margin of the resolution nobody would read, "president: elected separately, fixed term" and beneath it, "prime minister: chosen by Parliament, falls with it," then drew a question mark between the two lines, and looked up to vote.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 2022 the United Kingdom had three prime ministers, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak, without a general election, because the governing party changed its leader.
story:
The folding chairs in the city hall annex had been arranged in a horseshoe, and Victor set his notepad on the one nearest the podium because his hands shook less when he had something to hold. He had signed up for the youth civics forum three weeks ago, mostly because his counselor said colleges liked it, and only afterward discovered that the afternoon's exercise required him to argue a position he hadn't chosen. The moderator, a grad student with a clipboard, had dealt him parliamentary systems and told him to prepare to defend them against a girl named Priya, who would argue for presidential ones.

Priya was already there, her notes color-coded, and she nodded at him the way people nod at opponents before a match. "You want to rehearse once?" she asked. "My uncle lives in Manchester, so I've got material." Victor said sure, though his material consisted of half a page of bullet points copied from the library's encyclopedia the night before, and the strongest of them was a sentence about efficiency that he didn't fully understand himself.

They began in the corner by the water cooler, quietly, while the other pairs argued about electoral colleges and vote counting. Priya opened with the United States, with the fixed four-year term and the separation of powers, and Victor countered weakly that a prime minister could act faster because the legislature usually supported him. She let that pass. Then she leaned in, almost kindly. "Here's my best card. In 2022 the United Kingdom had three prime ministers in a single year. Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak. And none of them came in through a general election, because the governing party just changed its leader." She said it slowly, the way you deal a winning hand. "Your system picks a head of government nobody voted for. Twice. In one year."

Victor wrote the names down because his first instinct was that she had to be exaggerating. Johnson, Truss, Sunak. Three in one year.
