He asked whether there had been some crisis, some scandal, and she shrugged and said it didn't matter for her argument; what mattered was that the voters hadn't chosen. He wanted to argue and found he couldn't, because the fact sat there, solid and strange, and he didn't yet know what it proved or didn't prove.

The moderator called them to the horseshoe at four o'clock. Priya went first, and she was trenchant, laying out the case with clean, cutting precision: a president is chosen by the whole people, on a known schedule, and cannot be swapped out by party insiders. When she delivered the 2022 example, heads around the circle turned toward Victor with something between pity and appetite. He looked at his notes and understood, suddenly, that they were useless, because he had copied conclusions without ever having compared anything.

So he stopped reading. "I want to concede part of it," he said, and heard the room shift, surprised. "Three prime ministers in one year, chosen by a party instead of the country. That's a real cost. I'm not going to pretend it isn't." Priya's eyebrows rose, but she didn't interrupt. "But notice what it means. A presidential system has to wait years for a correction. The parliamentary one can act inside months. Whether that's worth it depends on what you're most afraid of, and I don't think the fear is the same everywhere." He could feel his own argument assembling itself as he spoke, two perspectives he had been holding apart clicking together like the halves of something he hadn't known was broken.

An older student across the horseshoe, the one everyone called an egoist because he turned every discussion toward himself, raised his hand to say the whole question was pointless since no system mattered next to the people in it. Victor surprised himself by answering that institutions shape which people get power in the first place, which was either profound or obvious, and the moderator wrote something on her clipboard either way.

Afterward, Priya found him by the door, coat already on. "You didn't really win," she said. "The fact still stands." Victor agreed that it did. He told her that what he'd figured out wasn't that her side was wrong, only that the same fact could mean instability to one person and responsiveness to another, and that he genuinely didn't know yet which weight mattered more, and that this bothered him less than it had that morning. She considered this with her chin tilted, then said his concession in the second minute had been smarter than it sounded, because it had emancipated him from defending the indefensible and left him free to argue the rest.

They walked out together into the plaza, where the city hall steps were still hung with banners from some earlier ceremony, and Priya said her uncle in Manchester had texted her a joke in 2022 about needing a program to keep track of the players. Victor said he wanted to read more before the next forum, actual books instead of encyclopedia entries, and asked what she was arguing next month. She said the Electoral College, and that he should pick the other side again, because he was better when he was losing. "I'm not sure that's a compliment," Victor said, and she laughed, and the automatic doors closed behind them with a soft pneumatic sigh.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When entering a highway, drivers use the acceleration lane to reach a speed close to that of highway traffic before merging, since merging slowly forces others to brake.
story:
The cones in Grandpa's driveway were meant to stand for parked cars, though they stood for nothing so well as his patience, which had survived two wars of attrition with Dylan's older cousins and their own driving tests. Dylan had been failing at the gap between them for three evenings now, easing the car in at an angle that was always either too timid or too aggressive, kissing the back cone with the bumper, then overcorrecting until the tires chewed the gravel at the road's edge.

"You're treating it like a geometry problem," Grandpa said from the porch, where he sat with coffee he never finished. "Some pithy little formula. It's not a formula. It's a rhythm."

"It is a formula," Dylan said, hand still on the wheel, though the engine was off. He had tried to parametrize the whole maneuver that morning in his notebook: distance from the curb, angle of entry, number of turns of the wheel, a curve drawn in pencil that looked, in the event, nothing like what the car did. The paper promised precision the steering column refused to deliver. His driving test was in nine days, and the test route, according to a cousin's worn recollection, included both parallel parking and a short hop onto Route 9.

"Then your formula's wrong," Grandpa said.

That was all he ever gave. Dylan's father would have taken the passenger seat and narrated the whole thing, hand hovering near the wheel, his instructions arriving like weather. Grandpa's silence was harder and, Dylan was beginning to admit, better. He reset the cones a foot closer together, the way the actual test would, and this time he didn't look at the back cone at all. He looked at the curb. He watched the rear tire in the mirror, turned the wheel once, twice, and slid in with a gap he could measure with his palm. The car settled level. Neither cone moved.

"There," he said aloud, to no one.

Route 9 was a different animal. The on-ramp by the grain co-op was long and curved, and the first time Dylan took it, with Grandpa beside him in the Buick's vast seat, he did what every instinct told him to do: he slowed down. Cars were coming in the right lane, a truck and then a silver hatchback, and his foot drifted off the gas as though caution were the same thing as safety. The hatchback's brake lights flared. Its driver leaned on the horn and swung into the left lane, and Dylan merged into a gap that was generous only because someone else had been forced to make it so.

His face was hot the whole way to the exit. "I panicked," he said.

"You decided slow was safe," Grandpa said, which was not the same sentence, and Dylan turned it over for two days.

On Thursday he drove the ramp again, alone in his thinking, Grandpa riding along. Halfway up the curve he caught himself lifting off the gas, the old reflex, and this time he pressed down instead. He understood it suddenly and completely: the ramp was an acceleration lane, and its whole purpose was to reach a speed close to that of the highway traffic before merging, because a slow merger forced everyone behind to brake. The hatchback's lights, the horn, the swerve, all of it had been the predictable cost of his caution. Speeding up was the safer choice. It felt like the opposite, and that was exactly the trap.

He came down the ramp at fifty-five, matched the flow of the truck's wake, and slid into the right lane without a single brake light blooming behind him. The mirrors stayed clear. Nobody honked. It was, he thought, almost anticlimactic, the way true things often were.

"Better," Grandpa said, which in his vocabulary was a paragraph.

They drove north past the co-op and the shuttered creamery, and Dylan held the lane steady and thought about the two lessons sitting side by side in him, unwilling to merge. In the driveway, slowness had been the discipline that saved him; on the ramp, slowness was the danger he had to accelerate out of. He could not make one rule out of them. Maybe the pithy version, the version his father would coin at dinner, was that safety was contextual, but Dylan distrusted anything that tidy. What he trusted was the feel of it: the curb in the mirror, the pedal under his foot, the gap that opened for you when you moved at the world's speed and closed against you when you didn't. Which was which, and when, he would have to learn again every time he got behind a wheel. He suspected that was the actual test.

At the top of the street, the cones waited in the driveway, spaced exactly as the examiner would space them. Dylan pulled past them, stopped, and checked his mirror.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: On many ocean current maps, warm currents are drawn with red arrows and cold currents with blue arrows.
story:
Sarah spread the ocean current map across the picnic table and weighted its curling corners with a jar of pickles, a flip-flop, and her brother's dour garden gnome, whose painted scowl suggested he had opinions about geography. The assignment was due Monday: explain, in one page, how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. She had a paragraph and a half and no idea what the squiggles on the map were actually telling her.

Her little brother Marcus, eleven and newly obsessed with weather disasters, looked over her shoulder. "Why's that arrow so red? Is it fast?"

"That's what I thought too," Sarah said. "But Mr. Okafor marked my practice quiz wrong when I said the red ones were speedsters."

"So what is it?"

"I don't know yet. That's the project." She tapped the wide red ribbon curling up from the Gulf of Mexico toward the North Atlantic, then the blue arrows snaking down the east side. If red meant fast, the map was saying the water left the Caribbean in a screaming hurry and then, apparently, sulked. If red meant something else, she needed to know what, because the whole page depended on it.

Marcus solved his part of the problem by lying in the hammock and narrating shark attacks to the gnome. Sarah worked. She turned her phone's weather app into a detective's tool, comparing places at the same latitude: Lisbon warm, Boston snowy, both practically neighbors on the globe's belt. She read, slowly, the caption she'd skimmed twice, and stopped. On many ocean current maps, warm currents were drawn with red arrows and cold currents with blue arrows. Not speed. Temperature. She sat back, half laughing at herself. She'd been reading a thermometer as a speedometer for a week.

"Marcus. Guess what's warm."

"Toast."

"The red arrows. Warm water. The blue ones are cold. That's the whole code."

Marcus sat up in the hammock with the gravity of a dissident who has just been told the regime was imaginary all along. "So the map I showed Danny, where I said the blue ones were slow, was wrong?"

"Danny thinks the California current is lazy because of you."

"It's not lazy?"

"It's cold. It could be very fast and very cold. Like a penguin."

Marcus took this seriously, as he took everything, and disappeared inside. He returned ten minutes later with a folded note, because their mother confiscated phones at six o'clock and Marcus considered the rule an injustice. He handed it over with ceremony, then went back to his sharks.

Sarah unfolded it. In pencil, in handwriting like a ransom demand, it said: "to Danny. correction. the blue arrows are not slow they are COLD. the red ones are warm. this is why europe is not frozen like canada even though its the same height. also I am still right about the sharks. signed Marcus." Below that, smaller: "is this right Sarah check before I send it."

She checked it against the caption, against the map, against the paragraph she'd been stuck on all afternoon, and the stuckness broke loose. The Gulf Stream was warm, red on the map, hauling heat north and east across the Atlantic like a conveyor of borrowed summers, and that was why her Lisbon-and-Boston comparison worked, why palm trees grew in Ireland at the same latitude as Newfoundland's ice. She was mesmerized by the sudden simplicity of it, one warm ribbon, one explanation, and she wrote the second half of the page right there at the picnic table, the pickle jar holding down her notebook while the wind tried to steal it.

She added a line at the bottom of Marcus's note, "yes it's right, don't mention penguins," and folded it back along his creases. Then she carried it across the yard, past the hammock, past the gnome standing guard like a small and disapproving customs official, and knocked on the fence gate that led to Danny's yard.

"Message for Danny," she called. "Courier service. One shark fact, corrected."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The force on a charge in an electric field equals the charge times the field strength, F = qE, so doubling the charge doubles the force.
story:
The physics gallery smelled like the inside of a hair dryer, air so desiccated by the dehumidifiers that Addison's lips cracked within ten minutes of walking in. She had come for extra credit, which was the official reason, and because Marcus from her physics class had said the new electrostatics exhibit was worth the bus fare, which was the unofficial one. Marcus was there already, leaning over a table where two brass plates sat parallel to each other, a hand-cranked generator beside them, and a small sign that read, in polite museum letters, "Field Between Plates: 500 volts across 2 centimeters."

"You're late," Marcus said.

"I'm exactly on time. You're early, which is a different thing." She set her notebook on the rail and copied the numbers. Five hundred volts. Two centimeters, so 0.02 meters. She had studied the formula on the ride over, the way you study a map on a train, trusting it would mean more once she arrived. Field strength is voltage divided by distance. She wrote 500 over 0.02 and worked it out, twice, because the decimal point had a way of sliding on her.

"Twenty-five thousand," she said. "Volts per meter. That's the field strength between the plates."

"That's what I got." Marcus sounded faintly disappointed that she had caught up, then recovered. "Okay, but here's the thing. So what? It's just a number until you do something with it."

A docent in a navy polo drifted past, straightening a stack of worksheets, but she didn't offer help, and Addison didn't ask. The last time an adult had explained something to her in a museum, it had been a man at the planetarium who called himself an astronomer and then mixed up two constellations, and her father had muttered "charlatan" all the way to the parking lot. She preferred to work it out herself anyway, even when it took longer, even when it shouldn't have taken as long as it did.

The exhibit had a clear plastic case between the plates, and inside the case, dust particles drifted and clung to surfaces, holding their tiny charges in the dry air. A magnifier built into the case's side let you watch them. Addison pressed her eye to it and saw a single pale fleck hovering, trembling, and beside the magnifier a small plaque: "A dust particle here carries a charge of one nanocoulomb."

"Marcus. The force on it. That's the something we can do."

He leaned in over her shoulder. "How?"

She thought about the formula she'd memorized and never used. Force equals charge times field strength. She had copied it into her notes as a line of symbols, F = qE, inert as a dead language, and now here was a real charged thing in a real field, waiting. She did the arithmetic on the corner of the page, converting nanocoulombs to coulombs because Mr. Okafor was merciless about units, and came out with something on the order of tens of micronewtons.

"It's a tiny push," she said. "But it's a real push. The field pushes on the charge."

"So if the dust had more charge," Marcus said slowly, watching the fleck through the magnifier, "it would get pushed harder."

"Right. Double the charge, double the force. It just multiplies." She said it and then paused, because saying it aloud made it suddenly visible to her, like a pattern in a floor you'd walked across for years. The whole formula was only multiplication. The field she'd computed from the plates, the charge on the dust, and the force linking them, and the linking was nothing stranger than proportion. She had spent three weeks treating physics as a set of incantations, and here it turned out to be arithmetic wearing a costume.

"You look weird," Marcus said. "Like you just found religion."

"I found out I already knew something and didn't know I knew it."

He turned the crank on the generator, and between the plates the dust fleck lurched sideways and stuck to a plate with a click she felt more than heard. A kid of maybe nine elbowed up to the rail, staring at the stuck fleck.

"It jumped," the kid said. "Why did it jump?"

"Because it had a charge, and the field pushed it," Addison said. "The force on a charge in a field is the charge times the field strength." The kid looked at her like she'd spoken Urdu, and she tried again. "It's like the dust is carrying something small, and the field is the wind. The more it carries, the harder the wind pushes it."

The kid nodded, satisfied or pretending, and wandered toward the Van de Graaff generator, where someone's hair was already rising. Marcus said, "You know you still can't tell me why the field is there in the first place. Why voltage over distance gives you anything at all."

"I know," she said. "I can compute it and use it and I still can't tell you why it's true. That's the part that keeps me up a little." She said it without embarrassment, which surprised her; a month ago she would have hidden the gap in her understanding rather than stand in front of it. Maybe the judicious move was to admit which things she knew and which she only trusted, and to keep the two lists separate in her notes.

She wrote at the bottom of her page: F = qE, double q, double F, and underlined it once, then closed the notebook and put the cap back on her pen.

"Extra credit box is by the exit," Marcus said. "You going to put the whole derivation in?"

"I'm going to put in what I actually did." She squared the pages together. "Field, dust, force. All of it observed."

At the exit, she dropped her worksheet into the slot marked submissions, and through the window in the door she could still see the two brass plates, the small clear case, the dust waiting to jump.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: All 50 US states and Washington, DC allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age.
story:
Elizabeth had agreed to run the peer health workshop mostly because Priya had promised there would be snacks, and only afterward did she understand that the snacks were for the audience and she would be the one talking. For three days the index cards on her desk multiplied like something from a lab experiment gone wrong. Consent, said one card, as if the word would explain itself. Contraception, said another, in handwriting that got smaller as her confidence did.

Her little brother Marcus leaned in her doorway on Thursday night, eating cereal dry from the box like a raccoon with a pantry. "You're going to stand up in front of thirty sophomores and say words out loud," he said. "Out loud, Elizabeth."

"They've heard the words."

"They've heard the words from Coach Riley, who calls everything 'the situation.' You have to actually explain it." He crunched, dour as a judge. "Also you should practice on me. I'm a hostile audience."

"You're fourteen."

"Sophomores are basically fourteen."

So she practiced on him, and it went badly, and then less badly. She learned that "consent is an ongoing agreement that either person can withdraw at any time" sounded like an aphorism until she gave it a situation, a couple of actual people deciding and changing their minds, and then Marcus said, "Oh, that's just not being a jerk about it," which was not the vocabulary she'd use on Saturday but was, she had to admit, the correct idea underneath.

The clinic part was the part she hadn't solved. She had a slide that said KNOW YOUR SERVICES and a diagram of a condom that she'd drawn herself and that Marcus had said looked like a sad jellyfish, and she knew she should say something about getting tested, but the fact she had in her head was vague and secondhand: somewhere, at some point, she'd absorbed the belief that a parent had to sign something. She kept imagining a sixteen-year-old in the front row asking "Do I have to tell my mom?" and herself standing there with a jellyfish diagram and no answer.

Then Rosa texted her on Friday night. Rosa, who had been her lab partner freshman year and now worked Saturdays at the public library, sent: ok weird question. do you know if a clinic will call my mom if i get tested? i asked google and google gave me a pamphlet from 1997 and a forum where a man named gary talks about garlic.

Rosa had a boyfriend now, Rosa was careful, Rosa was also sixteen and, as she put it, "a person who likes being sure of things, and right now I am sure of nothing." Elizabeth sat on her bed with the phone warm in her hand and thought of her mother, who historicized everything, who could not discuss any subject, from bus fares to breakfast cereal, without first explaining how people had felt about it in 1974. Elizabeth loved this about her and also, sometimes, wanted one plain sentence about the present.

"Come with me tomorrow," she texted. "There's a clinic two blocks from the library. I'll go with you and we'll just ask."

The waiting room had a fish tank with exactly one fish, enormous and orange, drifting like a retired mayor. Rosa filled out the form with her pen gripped tight enough to whiten her knuckles, and at the line where she'd expected a parent's signature she found nothing, and she looked up at the nurse, a small woman with reading glasses on a beaded chain, and said, "Nobody has to sign this? Like, my mom doesn't have to sign this?"

"All fifty states and DC let minors consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections on their own," the nurse said, tapping the clipboard. "No parent's permission needed. Some states do set a minimum age, but you're past it, and anyway we're not in one of those."

"Every state," Rosa said. "Even the ones that seem like they wouldn't."

"Even those. It's the law, not a favor."

Rosa exhaled so loudly that the fish turned to look at her, or seemed to. Elizabeth wrote the whole thing on the back of a receipt, under the jellyfish diagram, which she would redraw.

On Saturday Elizabeth stood in front of thirty sophomores with a plate of granola bars and a new card. She did the consent part with two volunteers and a scenario about borrowing a hoodie, which got a laugh and then, unexpectedly, a serious silence when the hoodie's owner said "actually, give it back" and the other kid did, immediately, and Elizabeth said, "That. That's the whole thing." She did contraception plainly, method by method, without blushing, though her ears went pink anyway and a girl in the second row said, "Your ears are doing it," kindly.

Then the question came, from a boy in a track jacket, exactly the question she'd been afraid of two nights ago: "Do our parents have to, like, sign a form or whatever?"

"Every state in the country, plus DC, a minor can consent to testing and treatment for STIs on their own. No parent signature. Some states have a minimum age, so it's worth knowing yours, but that's the shape of it." She paused. "I learned that yesterday. I thought it was the other way, and I was wrong, and now I'm not."

Afterward Rosa waited by the door with her backpack on one shoulder. "You said 'the shape of it,'" she said. "Very historic."

"My mom says that."

"Your mom would historicize a bus ticket." Rosa held up her phone, showing the clinic's follow-up text, everything clear, everything fine. "Come on. The fish tank lady said we could visit the fish anytime."

"Does the fish have a name?"

"Gary," Rosa said. "But he doesn't talk about garlic."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal distance a projectile travels equals its constant horizontal velocity multiplied by its time in the air.
story:
The launcher stood at the far end of the physics hall, past the Tesla coil and the pendulum sandbox, and Hayden had walked past it a dozen times on school trips without stopping. Today he stopped, because on Monday there would be a test, and on Monday he would have to find where a ball landed when it was fired at some angle at some speed, and he did not know how. The exhibit had a yellow pneumatic gun, a protractor dial, and a floor marked off in numbered squares, and beside it a plaque that said, in cheerful museum font, PREDICT BEFORE YOU SHOOT.

He set the dial to thirty degrees. A small screen reported the launch speed, twelve meters per second, and offered a hint in exchange for pressing a green button, but Hayden didn't press it. He took out his phone, opened the notes app, and wrote v equals twelve, angle equals thirty. Then he stared at the screen for a long time, because after that he had nothing. His teacher had said something in class about components, about splitting the velocity into pieces, and Hayden had copied it down without understanding it, the way he copied a lot of things down, trusting that meaning would arrive later, the way a package arrives whether or not you watch the road.

A girl about his age was watching him from the bench by the pendulum, a stroller parked beside her, a toddler asleep inside it. "You're doing homework at the launcher," she said. It wasn't quite a question.

"I'm trying to," Hayden said. "I know the speed. I know the angle. I don't know where it lands."

"Neither does the floor," she said, "until the ball tells it." She stood up, checked the toddler, and came over. "I'm Rosa. My sister sleeps through everything, which is the only reason I get to come here."

He told her the plan the exhibit wanted, predict before you shoot, and she said fine, but you have to actually predict, out loud, square number. The rule felt visceral to him, the fear of being wrong in front of a stranger in a public place, and he almost packed up the phone. Instead he drew a right triangle in his notes, the hypotenuse labeled twelve, and remembered, suddenly and completely, what his teacher had drawn on the board: the vertical piece and the horizontal piece, and how the sine and cosine divided the speed between them. Vertical was sine, twelve times sin thirty, which was six. Horizontal was cosine, twelve times cos thirty. He did the arithmetic on the phone. Ten point four, roughly.

"Okay," he said. "Ten point four meters per second sideways. Six up." He knew the up-and-down part from class, the way gravity drains vertical speed, the way you can find how long the ball stays in the air. He worked it, erased it, worked it again, interpolating between the too-neat numbers his memory supplied until he had something he trusted a little. "It's in the air about one point two seconds."

"So it lands at square twelve," Rosa said, pointing at the floor grid, and he said no, wait, and then he saw it, and the seeing of it was so plain it embarrassed him. The ball moves sideways the whole time it's in the air, and sideways it never slows down, not in the world where the plaque's math lives. Ten point four meters every second, one point two seconds. "About twelve and a half meters," he said. "Square thirteen. The distance is just the sideways speed times the time in the air." Rosa wrote the number on the little whiteboard hanging from the rail, the way the exhibit asked, in her handwriting, because he said his would look like a forgery of competence.

He fired the launcher. The ball rose in the arc he had imagined, hung at the top where the vertical speed ran out, and fell into the far edge of square thirteen. Rosa made a sound like a struck bell. The toddler did not wake. Hayden stood there feeling the odd doubleness of it, that the neat equation on his phone and the actual rubber ball in the actual air were the same event seen two ways, that the world could be argued with in numbers and would sometimes agree. He had always thought of math as a language for machines and museums, not for a Tuesday afternoon with a stranger watching.

Then came the twist, which was that Rosa pressed the green hint button before he could stop her, and the screen displayed the official answer: twelve meters, square twelve, launch speed twelve point four, not twelve. His launch speed had been rounded on the display. He recalculated with the true speed and got a landing point a fraction short of what the ball had actually done, and stared at the small mismatch, half a square of disagreement between the clean world and the real one. "Air," Rosa said, shrugging, as though that settled it, and maybe it did, and maybe it didn't. "Try forty-five degrees," she added, going back to the stroller. "I'll hold the whiteboard. You do the logos, I'll do the pen."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.
story:
The thermometer read 31 degrees, and Audrey held it like a verdict. Tomorrow morning her grandmother's boxes would arrive from the auction house, and tonight was the only night she had to fill the moulds she'd bought with her first paycheck: twelve half-shells of dark chocolate, one for each cousin at Sunday's farewell lunch before she left for college. Her mother had offered to buy chocolates from the shop on Delancey. Audrey had said no with a stubbornness that surprised them both.

She had a method, or what passed for one. She'd watched a video four times, paused at each temperature, and copied the numbers onto an index card as if she could codify the whole craft into a sequence she could follow blindly: melt to 45, cool to 27, warm back to 31. What the card didn't say was what the chocolate was doing in between, and so she stirred and waited and stirred, wondering whether there was a way to know temper by something other than a thermometer's word. The video had mentioned a smear test on marble, a shine that appeared like an answer, but her kitchen had no marble, only the enamel counter with its chipped corner, and the chocolate on her spatula stayed matte and slow.

At 31 degrees exactly she poured. The shells went into the fridge, and she sat on the floor beside it with the timer set for twenty minutes, listening to the compressor hum. There was something in the process that made her want to laugh at herself: all this ceremony, this precision, for chocolate that would be eaten in an afternoon. Her little brother Theo wandered in for milk and stood over the moulds with the frank appraisal of a ten-year-old.

"Grandma used to make these," he said. "Hers came out of the moulds like coins. Shiny." He tapped the plastic. "Yours look cloudy."

"That's the fridge's fault," Audrey said, though she wasn't sure it was. She turned one mould over and tapped the back the way the video had shown. Nothing moved. She tapped harder, then pried at an edge with a fingernail, and the shell came out dull and broken, a crescent of chocolate still wedged in the cavity like a tooth.

She sat back on her heels. Theo drank his milk and watched her fail, which was its own kind of patience. Audrey turned the broken shell over in her fingers, and the question arrived quietly, the way useful questions did: why had the video promised that tempered chocolate would release on its own? She replayed the woman's voice in her head, the certainty of it. "Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets," the woman had said, "which helps it release cleanly from a mould." Shrinks. Pulls itself away from the walls. Her shells hadn't shrunk; they'd set soft and clingy, holding the plastic like they were afraid of it. Which meant, and the logic assembled itself as she stared at the wreckage, that the chocolate had never been in temper at all. The thermometer had said 31. The chocolate had said otherwise, and she'd only asked the thermometer.

"I think I skipped a step," she said. "Or the step didn't count. Like when you follow a recipe and it turns out someone else's oven runs hot."

"So do it again," Theo said, as if this were obvious and slightly entertaining.

She checked the clock. Eleven. The leftover chocolate sat in the bowl in a dull slab, and she would have to start over from the beginning, melt it all the way up again. There was a part of her that wanted to treat the failure as a verdict on her, on the whole plan, on the profligate waste of an evening and two hundred grams of good couverture. But another part of her, the part that had liked chemistry and liked it precisely for the moments when the second attempt worked, said the failure was information. The first batch had taught her what out-of-temper looked like: matte, soft, clingy. So temper was the absence of that, plus the shine, plus, if the video was right, that slight shrinking she hadn't believed until her broken shell proved it from the negative side. Two ways of knowing, really, the numbers on her card and the behavior of the chocolate itself, and neither one enough alone. She got up and set the bowl over the water bath.

The second time she watched instead of only measuring. As the chocolate cooled toward 27, she pulled the spatula across the counter's cool enamel and waited ten seconds; the streak set with a snap and a faint satin sheen, and she laughed out loud at how obvious it was, how the chocolate had been willing to tell her everything all along if she'd known how to look. Theo came back in his pajamas to see what was funny, and she let him smear a test stripe himself. His set too.

"Is it alive?" he asked, poking the streak.

"No," she said. "It just acts like it wants things. Fat molecules arranging themselves, or something. I don't fully get it yet." That last part came out easier than she expected. She poured the shells again, tapped out the bubbles, and slid the mould into the fridge, and then she sat on the floor with her back against the door and set the timer for twenty minutes. When it buzzed she turned the mould over, held her breath, and gave it one sharp knock.

The shells dropped onto the plate in a bright, snapping tumble, whole, and Theo reached for one before she could stop him.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1859, John Tyndall began laboratory experiments measuring how gases absorb infrared heat, showing that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb it while nitrogen and oxygen do not.
story:
The trail to the campground ran out of gravel a mile early, so Marcus walked the last stretch with the cooler while his father carried the tent, neither of them speaking except to point out roots. It had been his father's idea, this trip, offered in the flat voice he used since the divorce papers, and Marcus had agreed mostly because refusing seemed like a decision he would have to explain. In his pack, wrapped in a towel between two shirts, he had a library book about the history of climate science, checked out for a report due the second week of college, a report he was quietly afraid of because he did not yet understand the thing he was supposed to explain.

He understood the assignment as a sentence: describe how greenhouse gases trap heat, and interpret a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century. He had printed the graph and folded it into the book, and the graph looked simple enough, a line rising steeply near the right edge, but whenever he tried to say out loud why the line rose or what it meant, his own voice sounded like a paraphrase of someone else's confidence. He had learned by now that repeating a thing was not the same as holding it.

That evening his cousin Elena arrived from the neighboring site, seventeen like him, already accepted to a school in Ohio, carrying a bag of marshmallows and the particular energy of someone who wanted to talk. They sat on the cooler while the fire built itself down to coals. She asked what he was reading, and when he showed her the cover she made a face.

"Climate change," she said. "That's such a now thing. Like, everything about it is new, the data, the arguments, all of it. My uncle thinks the whole idea was invented so scientists could get funding."

Marcus turned to the chapter he had read twice on the drive up. "It's older than that," he said. "There was this guy, John Tyndall. In 1859 he started doing laboratory experiments measuring how gases absorb infrared heat. Water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb it. Nitrogen and oxygen don't."

Elena stopped with a marshmallow halfway onto a stick. "Eighteen fifty-nine?"

"That's what it says. He built the apparatus himself. In a lab. Before cars, before any of it."

She turned this over with the visible effort of someone rearranging furniture in a small room. Her uncle's whole position rested on newness, on the idea that this was a modern invention, and here was a Victorian experiment sitting underneath it like bedrock. She asked to see the page, and he held the book toward the firelight, and she read it herself, slowly, mouthing some of it.

Later, when Elena had gone back to her site and his father had fallen asleep in the tent with the audacity of a man who had nothing due in September, Marcus sat with the headlamp and the folded graph and worked at the thing he could not do. He laid the paper flat on the picnic table and weighted the corners with stones still warm from the fire. The line began low and level on the left, the century's early decades, then bent upward, then bent again, steeper, until the last decades climbed almost vertically. He had assumed, at first, that reading a graph meant describing its shape. Now he tried something different, the way Tyndall's experiment demanded a different kind of attention. He put his finger at 1859 and thought: the man had measured this in a laboratory before anyone had a reason to want it to be untrue. Then he traced the line forward through the years his grandparents were born, his parents, him, and let the two ideas sit together, the small nineteenth-century measurement and the long upward sweep.

The cold invigorated him after an hour of stillness; he stood and rolled his shoulders and felt the clarity that comes with exhaustion honestly earned. The graph had acquired a kind of gravitas for him now, not because of what anyone said about it but because a line drawn from so many scattered measurements, gathered by so many hands over so many years, could only be ignored by pretending each hand was lying separately. At the same time he noticed, with a smaller and more stubborn honesty, what he still could not claim. He could not say how much of the rise was owed to what, could not defend the details against Elena's uncle, and when he tried to picture the actual motion of heat through air, the picture dissolved into a gray blur he was borrowing from diagrams he half-remembered.

In the morning his father was up early, boiling water, moving with the deliberate calm of a man attempting to demonstrate that he was fine. He asked, without looking over, whether Marcus had gotten his schoolwork done by the fire, and there was something underneath the question, an old argument about whether a camping trip should be a place for books, or possibly an older one about whether Marcus took things too seriously, the way his mother had. Marcus considered deflecting. Instead he carried the graph over and set it on the table between the mugs.

"That line's carbon dioxide over the last hundred years," he said. "I have to explain it for a report. I can explain most of it. Some of it I can't yet."

His father looked at the paper for a long moment, steam rising off the pot behind him, and the sunlight came down through the pines in stripes across the rising edge of the line.

"So what's the part you can't explain?" he asked.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: A few drops of water in melted chocolate can make it seize into a thick, grainy paste, because the sugar and cocoa particles clump together.
story:
Violet had promised forty truffles for the Saturday market, and by seven in the morning she had ruined every ounce of chocolate she owned. The stall smelled like a bakery that had lost an argument with itself, and her aunt Rosa, who ran the table two rows over near the honey jars, kept glancing over with the particular patience of someone waiting for a young person to ask for help.

The trouble had come fast. She had set a bowl of chopped chocolate over a pot of simmering water, the way the internet showed, and gone to answer a text about the folding tables. When she came back, the steam had done its quiet work, condensing on the bottom of the bowl and the rim of the pot, and a few drops had fallen in. The chocolate, which moments before had flowed like warm caramel, had turned stiff and grainy, a thick paste that clung to her spatula in a dull gray slab. She stared at it as if it had insulted her on purpose.

"It seized," said Marisol, the fourteen-year-old who worked the flower stall and had wandered over for the free samples that were not coming. "My mom says that. A few drops of water in melted chocolate and it seizes, goes all thick and grainy, because the sugar and cocoa clump together." She peered into the bowl. "That's seized, all right."

Violet did not want a chemistry lecture from someone who still had braces, but she also wanted to sell something today, and those two wants did not fit in the same head comfortably. She scraped the ruined paste into a container, labeled it SEIZED in her incisive, slanted handwriting, and set it aside, because her mother had spent years trying to inculcate the habit of naming failures instead of burying them, and sometimes, at inconvenient hours, the lesson actually held.

What she had left was one bag of couverture, the good stuff, and forty minutes before the market filled. The trouble was that untempered chocolate, when it set, went soft and streaky and bent instead of snapping. Rosa had shown her once, in June: a bar held at an angle and broken cleanly, the fracture line glossy as a mirror. Violet had broken her own attempts and gotten a sad, waxy bend, chocolate with the posture of a lecture. She wanted the snap. She wanted to hand a customer a truffle that cracked like it meant it.

So she improvised a second attempt, dry this time, no double boiler at all, just the bowl set on a towel far from the steam, coaxed gently over the pot's rising heat and then pulled away. She tested the temperature against her wrist like a bottle for an infant, because her thermometer had cracked last week and she had not replaced it, a piece of pedantry she now regretted since thermometers were, in fact, not pedantry at all but basic equipment. She stirred. She stirred more, watching the chocolate cool and thicken slightly, and smeared a bit on the back of a spoon, waited, waited, then pressed her thumbnail into it. It dried in seconds with a satin sheen. She broke the spoon's coating off and it snapped, a small clean sound, and she heard herself laugh out loud, alone, which embarrassed her enough to look around.

The first customer was a man in a cycling kit who bought six truffles and ate one at the table immediately, breaking it with his teeth. "That's a proper snap," he said, and Violet felt the sentence land somewhere unreasonable in her chest, given that it was one stranger and one chocolate. She was not sure the second batch would work. The science of it stayed half dark to her; she had protected the bowl from steam and the chocolate had cooperated, but she could not have said exactly where the line was between a drop and a disaster, only that the line existed and she had stayed on the far side of it once.

Marisol came back at noon, ostensibly to buy a truffle, actually to collect her reward for the morning's diagnosis. Violet gave her two, and one extra for the seized intelligence. "You know what I did wrong," Violet said, holding up the labeled container, "and I wrote it down, and next week I'm buying a thermometer, and a lid." Marisol nodded and ate the truffle in two bites and said, "Still snappy," with her mouth full, which Violet decided to take as the highest available form of review.

By two o'clock the table was nearly empty and Rosa came over with a bag of plums and stood beside her in the flat afternoon light. Violet counted the cash box, recounted it, and told her aunt about the seizing, the steam, the improvised temper, the thumbnail test she had half invented and half remembered from a video. Rosa listened without correcting anything, which was her way of saying the account was probably close to true. "So next week," Rosa said, "same table?" Violet looked at the smeared, shining bowl, at the container marked SEIZED, at the last three truffles sitting in their paper cups. "Same table," she said, and put the lid on the box before the wind could get at them.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Circumlocution, describing a word you cannot remember instead of stopping, is a recognized communication strategy that keeps a second-language speaker talking.
story:
The assignment was taped to the door of Room 114: five minutes, in Spanish, on a current issue, no notes. Hailey read it twice, then copied it into her planner in the small square for Thursday, which was already crossed out and rewritten once, so that the week looked like a place where things had been thought better of.

Her topic was the city's plan to tax deliveries to fund bus lanes. She had opinions in English, a whole crowded shelf of them, but when she tried to move them into Spanish they arrived in pieces. Monday night she sat at the kitchen table building sentences out of a dictionary, and her mother leaned over her shoulder and asked what she was doing. "Trying to argue about taxes," Hailey said, "in a language where I don't have the word for taxes." Her mother made a noncommittal sound and went back to her crossword, but later she left a folded note beside Hailey's mug: "Your abuela used to say that when you lose a word, you borrow the whole story around it. She talked circles around English for forty years and everyone understood her." Hailey read the note three times, then folded it smaller and put it in her pocket without deciding what it meant.

Wednesday, in class, Mr. Ferrar only spoke Spanish, so half the room's confusion went politely unexpressed. He had them practice in pairs, two minutes each, and Hailey's partner, Denny, kept stopping mid-sentence whenever a word escaped him, like a man dropping his groceries and refusing to continue without every last apple. He stopped five times in two minutes. When he was done, breathless and flushed, he said in English, "I forgot the word for tax. What was I supposed to do, just stand there?"

Hailey found she had been watching him the way you watch a machine with one visible fault. "Stand there worse," she said slowly, not sure she believed it. "Or talk around it." Then, curious, she tried it. She set the timer again and began, and when the word for tax dissolved on her tongue she did not stop; she said, in her careful Spanish, "the money that the government takes from people and from companies, a part of what everyone earns," and kept going, and the sentence closed behind her like water over a dropped stone. Denny blinked at her. "That was actually good. It's like circumlocution, like from English class. Talking around a word." She hadn't thought of the term in years, and there it was, suddenly useful, the way old things sometimes are.

That night she made a list of the words she might lose: tax, delivery, congestion, fair. Next to each one she wrote a circle of other words, a net to catch the fall. But somewhere between the second and third entry she stopped, because a question she liked better had arrived. Which Hailey would be doing the talking on Thursday? There was the Hailey who argued with her father at dinner, quick, certain, fond of the phrase "if you think about it," which she used mostly when she had already finished thinking. And there was the Hailey of the kitchen table, who moved slowly through Spanish, who had to want each sentence before she could say it. In the second language she could not fake speed. She could only mean things at the pace she could build them. What she actually believed about the tax, she realized, she had never had to find out, because in English she could win without locating it.

Thursday came warm, and the windows of Room 114 were open, and the traffic on Delancey could be heard gearing up for its evening congestion, which felt like a stage prop provided by the city itself. Mr. Ferrar called her name and started the timer on the whiteboard, its numbers counting down in red. Hailey began. She said the plan was good for people who rode the bus, and hard on small shops, and that the money had to come from somewhere. At the fifty-second mark the word for tax left her entirely, a door closing quietly somewhere in her head. "The money that the government takes," she said, "a part of what people earn, from their remuneration," and she saw Denny, in the second row, nod once, like a coach.

She also said, in her plodding but honest Spanish, that she did not know yet whether the shops could bear it, that some people would impute bad motives to the council when maybe the council was only clumsy, and that five minutes was perhaps enough to describe a problem but not enough to solve one. When the timer hit zero she was mid-sentence, and she stopped where the sentence stopped, without adding a conclusion.

Mr. Ferrar wrote a number in his book, then said, in Spanish, "Sixty seconds more, if you want them. You were talking around one word for a while there." Hailey stood with her hands on the desk, feeling the offer sit in the air. Sixty seconds was long enough to take something back, or long enough to say the thing she had circled all week without landing on. "No," she said, and then, in English, because some words you keep in the first language, "I like where I stopped." She sat down, and Denny leaned over and whispered, "You forgot tax again, didn't you." "Twice," Hailey said, and grinned.
